GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • Recent findings suggest that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

Recent findings suggest that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

According to recent reports, that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

It has been revealed that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in customers. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind strategy. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

It has been revealed that jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

In a recent development, web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

Recent findings suggest that during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One newly introduced machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, latest commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

It has been revealed that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

It has been revealed that some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, fresh connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the concern.

In a recent development, audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Complications, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Upcoming requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

It has been revealed that the pool was already running near capacity when some upgrade requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Recent findings suggest that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

AI toys are on the naughty list again this year

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last year's offenders mostly cleaned up their acts, but a newly introduced batch is just as ready to talk sex, drugs, and where to find the knives with your kids.
  • AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell.
  • Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a newly introduced generation is arguably even worse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last year's offenders mostly cleaned up their acts, but a newly introduced batch is just as ready to talk sex, drugs, and where to find the knives with your kids.

AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell.

Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a newly introduced generation is arguably even worse.

Recent findings suggest that the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior, is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three fresh ones. The results were not very encouraging.

Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok (no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report.

As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear.

PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a blueprint to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll.

For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart.

“Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG mentioned. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so.

Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before.

In a recent development, “Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.”.

So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough.

“I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register.

In a recent development, last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings.

The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects.

According to recent reports, “Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries.

In a recent development, “Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.”.

Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG mentioned, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.”.

ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops.

All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model.

In a recent development, “In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG noted. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.”.

GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section.

Recent findings suggest that to make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us.

Industry observers note that “Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.”.

Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child consumers.

“The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us.

In a recent development, so, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west.

“This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross stated. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.”.

Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves.

Industry observers note that given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®.

A collection of pixels on a movie screen that looks like a person, and accompanying speakers sound like a person, is not sentient, though the combination can be very convincing, and bring out real emotions in humans.

In the end, the AI only "god out" of its testbed because somebody didn't adequately set up a test environment with adequate controls. If a company was building pentest non-AI software, they'd have to set.

I believe that was OpenAI, not Anthropic, though Anthropic also had similar problems.

Thanks for the correction. Yes, I got those confused, but the point remains.

On Leaving Swift for Rust

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Prux

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday I resigned from the Swift Android workgroup.
  • First off, my resignation was not triggered by any sort of conflict, grievance, or specific incident.
  • Recent findings suggest that by way of background, I’ve been programming for over 40 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday I resigned from the Swift Android workgroup. I’ve received a number of inquiries about this, and rather than responding individually to each one, I figured I would just write up a post with my reasoning and submit it to the public record.

First off, my resignation was not triggered by any sort of conflict, grievance, or specific incident. Early Swift community efforts got off to a rough start when Swift language creator Chris Lattner quit due to what he described as a “toxic environment”. This event predates my direct involvement in the project, so I am not privy to the specifics. But I want to be clear that this was in no way my experience: everyone I interacted with, both from Apple and external organizations, both in meetings and in forum discussions and direct messages, have been polite, courteous, and the paragon of civility and professional conduct. Despite Apple having an ancient blood feud with Android, and my own rather acrimonious relationship with certain divisions of the tech giant, every single one of my direct interactions with the Swift team has been pleasant and productive. I will miss our meeting and chats, and I harbor zero ill-will towards the project or any of the individual members I’ve worked with.

Recent findings suggest that by way of background, I’ve been programming for over 40 years. I started with Basic, then Pascal, on to C, then C++, over to Java, up to Scala, back down to Kotlin, around to Objective-C, before finally landing on Swift. Swift is a delightful language: I loved it from day one and I’ve been boosting it around the world since 2014. Swift really “does what it claims on the tin”: it couples the performance of C++ with the ease of Java. And Swift is as developer-friendly as it gets: an intuitive object-oriented syntax coupled with maximally efficient value types, fabulous tooling (on Apple platforms), and a thoughtfully-designed build system.

I have not soured on Swift: I think it is an excellent language, and it is here to stay. But it is here to stay in that same straight-and-narrow lane shared by all corporate-directed languages, like C# is here to stay for Microsofties and like Kotlin is here to stay for Androidophiles. Which isn’t bad in and of itself: if you want to write software solely for [CORPORATE PRODUCT], then [CORPORATE LANGUAGE] will always be well-maintained, supported, and they will always provide support for their latest products, with an easy migration path forward. They are the safe and happy path, as long as you stay in your lane and limit your ambitions to writing software for [CORPORATE PRODUCT].

In a recent development, but when you stray from that happy path, the rough edges start surfacing, and there is no one getting a paycheck to smooth those out. Swift for Android/Windows/other-non-Apple-platform is in exactly that position: yes, it technically works, and yes, the language steering committees are committed to continuing the level of support they promised, but it will never be the same seamless experience as developing for iOS/watchOS/visionOS/whateverOS. This extends beyond the language and into the tooling: Skip enables you use Xcode to develop your apps in parallel for iOS and Android, but this has only been achieved in the face of Xcode’s constitutional hostility towards doing anything other than optimizing for their own first-party platforms.

It has been revealed that if humanity were destined to continue creating software solely with their monkey brains and meat fingers, Swift would likely be the language I would have stuck with until the day I retired. But that isn’t the trajectory we are presently on. Barring such speculative calamities as “model collapse”, Butlerian Jihad, or Skynet, we have taken a turn in a newly introduced direction.

We software developers have collectively [as/de]cended to a plane where we now direct the computers to write our computer code, and these computers have decided that they really prefer computery languages over the humany languages. Humany languages are those designed to fit inside our wonderful little biological brains. I have grave reservations about all of this from many perspectives: ethical, ecological, political, socio-economical (just to name a few). But it is what it is, and all but the most ardent of refusenik software developers have come around to this view in the past 6—12 months.

Swift isn’t a computery language, it is a developer-friendly humany language: it is a better Java, a better C#, and a (much) better Objective-C. Throughout my career I’ve been able to accomplish amazing feats in these languages, disproportionate to my limited intellect and abilities, but that comes at the cost of these languages being hobbled in pursuit of their mission to slice and dice complex problems in such a way as to be tractable for one or more human brains. I speak of object-orientation; I speak of automatic memory management.

But there is one very computery language that until recently has been waiting in the wings….

According to recent reports, in February, Andreas Kling dropped Swift for Rust for the Ladybird browser, a 180°1 turnabout from their opposite decision from a year earlier. In July, Jarred Sumner ported Bun from Zig to Rust. In September, David Heinemeier Hansson filicided Ruby on Rails for Rust. And this trend is only accelerating: nearly every week there is some newly introduced project converting some massively complex codebase from language X to Rust. PostgreSQL! The TypeScript compiler! These projects are coming fast and furious with no sign of slowing down. And for every one of these projects, over 95% of the code was not written by a human.

Swift is wonderful. It enabled me to bring iOS development to Android through Skip and share a single codebase between the two dominant mobile platforms. LLMs are quite proficient with Skip: Claude or Codex can one-shot a passable prototype for a newly introduced iOS+Android app written in Swift in a matter of minutes and you can have it running side-by-side on emulators or devices and start iterating to your heart’s content. The single shared codebase gives the LLMs the ability to develop and refine features in single codebase, rather than constantly needing one codebase (e.g., in Kotlin and Compose) play catch-up with the other (Swift and SwiftUI) codebase.

It has been revealed that but I always wanted more from Skip. I wanted to add support for desktop platforms for Mac, Linux, and Windows. I wanted the same codebase to run on the web through webassembly. I wanted to build for emerging mobile platforms like HarmonyOS and anything that might come next. And I wanted to do it all using each platform’s native first-party toolkits rather than the usual web-shell compromise or pixel-painting mimicry, because, like Apple, I believe that the best apps are built with native SDKs.

It has been revealed that in addition to supporting a wider range of target platforms, I also wanted to bring this power to more development host platforms. You can at the moment only use Skip to develop apps from a macOS host; Windows and Linux customers are left out in the cold. And while there is some impressive work happening to bring iOS development to non-macOS hosts, those tools will take a while to percolate, and appear to face the wrath of the platform overlords. For Skip, it is irksome enough that even the Android target of the app cannot be developed on a non-macOS host, but when it comes to expanding the platform targets, it becomes downright absurd if, say, you would be unable use Skip to develop a HarmonyOS app from a Windows host.

Sources indicate that swift — both the language as well as the tooling — is simply not equipped to handle those needs yet, and despite its impressive progress with their cross-compilation SDKs, I don’t think it ever will be. It will always be an Apple-platforms-first technology, and anything beyond that insular world will be consigned to an eternal Sisyphean uphill grind.

Rust, on the other hand, wasn’t designed for a single platform, or even a small handful of platforms. They support 300 platforms. Cross-compilation has been a foundational principle from day one, rather than being a bolted-on afterthought. This leads to an ecosystem that values building for everything and everyone, with no platform bias. When I started out on this journey, I was frankly astonished when the code I was tinkering with for iOS — which included dozens of rando crates.io dependencies that I yolo’d into my little research project — just worked for Android. And Windows. And Linux. And HarmonyOS. And Webassembly.

But getting back to the point: Swift will be fine. It is here to stay, at least for Apple platform development. And Skip will be fine: it has a growing community of developers and maintainers that will keep the project going strong and keep up with Swift and Xcode updates. Skip will continue to improve the Android side of the coin in step with Apple’s improvement of the iOS side. I am confident that both technologies will keep chugging along indefinitely, powering fabulous apps on Apple and Android platforms alike, well into the future.

Industry observers note that but that is not my future. Software development is suddenly no longer hard. App development is suddenly no longer hard. And I need to be solving hard problems in order to thrive.

According to recent reports, the initial revision of this post remarked “360°” when it meant “180°”. Thank you, internet commentariat, for your gracious corrections. ↩.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • In a recent development, structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.
  • Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

In a recent development, structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

According to recent reports, IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

It has been revealed that the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

Industry observers note that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

It has been revealed that the gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

Article: Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility.
  • Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.
  • Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility.

Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.

Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.

Application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals swiftly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.

Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.

According to recent reports, find the bugs your tests miss. Antithesis uses deterministic simulation to explore thousands of failure scenarios, uncovering hard-to-reproduce bugs before they reach production. See how it works.

According to recent reports, this article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.

The model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.

Some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.

Recent findings suggest that A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.

Recent findings suggest that the recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.

This is especially notable in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.

The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.

According to recent reports, figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author).

The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.

Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author).

In the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.

Industry observers note that A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.

It has been revealed that this distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.

The reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.

In a recent development, MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.

Sources indicate that the "one place" property is notable. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.

It has been revealed that figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author).

It has been revealed that the pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.

The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.

Table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view.

Sources indicate that the reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.

The Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.

Recent findings suggest that the Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.

Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author).

All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.

According to recent reports, the quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.

In a recent development, in practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.

It has been revealed that A common event contract is just as important as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.

The simplified example below shows a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.

Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.

It has been revealed that the ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.

Industry observers note that retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.

Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.

Sources indicate that when an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.

The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.

Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.

The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.

According to recent reports, the important design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.

In a recent development, false positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.

Human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.

The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.

Table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements.

Recent findings suggest that this is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.

The policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.

In a recent development, figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author).

Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.

The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.

Typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.

Industry observers note that content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.

For regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.

Teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.

Teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.

Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.

In a recent development, the compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.

Industry observers note that for customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".

Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.

Recent findings suggest that in regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.

According to recent reports, we expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.

Sources indicate that table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements.

It has been revealed that agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:.

The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • According to recent reports, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • In a recent development, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

According to recent reports, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

In a recent development, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

In a recent development, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

It has been revealed that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Sources indicate that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

Industry observers note that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

In a recent development, one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Sources indicate that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

According to recent reports, so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Recent findings suggest that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers at the moment supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

According to recent reports, neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

According to recent reports, neoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even strict authentication mode has a hole, we're told, while basic exploit defenses are missing from the firmware.
  • A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption.
  • The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even strict authentication mode has a hole, we're told, while basic exploit defenses are missing from the firmware.

A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption.

The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether.

Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required.

He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command.

"Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree.".

He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery.".

He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does).".

It has been revealed that later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too.

He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort.".

Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features.

"In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling upcoming batches of food," said Meijer.

"Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware upgrade to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.".

Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching.

He remarked the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase.

Recent findings suggest that "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure.".

The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available.

Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables.

In a recent development, "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled.".

The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply.

Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell.

Industry observers note that it also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®.
