InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

Sources indicate that the agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post).

Industry observers note that an initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

This change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life currently set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:.

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

The legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post).

A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

It has been revealed that uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team aims to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

#23169. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • According to recent reports, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

According to recent reports, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

It has been revealed that this work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project indicated they were worth trying.

It has been revealed that before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

Recent findings suggest that v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

According to recent reports, A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

It has been revealed that the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Sources indicate that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

According to recent reports, BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

Sources indicate that A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Recent findings suggest that real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

It has been revealed that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Fresh words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

In a recent development, caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

According to recent reports, the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated fresh memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Recent findings suggest that small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

According to recent reports, repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on upcoming input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Sources indicate that both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

Industry observers note that A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

In a recent development, the benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

Industry observers note that the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has blessed seven C++ language revisions since 1998. The language is mostly developed by ISO's Working Group 21, which considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document, and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a standard. On October 23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed latest "contracts" feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.

#23167. The Smartest AI Decision Might Be Not Sending the Message

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1343 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

The Smartest AI Decision Might Be Not Sending the Message

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that generative AI has made it much cheaper to produce a personalized message.
  • It has been revealed that that distinction matters as AI takes on more of the decisions behind customer interactions.
  • Better writing won’t fix any of those problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that generative AI has made it much cheaper to produce a personalized message. It hasn’t made it easier to decide whether that message should be sent.

It has been revealed that that distinction matters as AI takes on more of the decisions behind customer interactions. A system can produce a relevant offer, predict that someone will click and still make the wrong decision. The customer may be waiting on a refund. They may have an unresolved complaint. They may have already bought the product under a different email address.

Better writing won’t fix any of those problems. The system needs a better understanding of the customer, an objective that reflects what the business actually values and clear limits on what it can do.

Sends, opens, and clicks are easy to count. That makes them useful operating metrics, but it also makes them tempting substitutes for the thing a business actually wants: a customer who sees value in the relationship and keeps coming back.

An AI system optimized for total clicks, with few constraints on contact frequency, may find that sending more messages improves its score. Each additional send can look reasonable in isolation. Across campaigns and channels, the same customer can end up hearing from the brand far more often than anyone intended.

It has been revealed that think about a customer who returned an order last week and is still waiting on a refund. A marketing system sees a recent purchaser with a high likelihood of responding and queues a promotional email. From the customer’s perspective, the brand is asking for more money before returning what it owes.

The return may live in the order system, the refund status in a service tool and the purchase in a marketing profile. Those records may not even be connected to the same person. The model can be working exactly as designed and still be making a decision from an incomplete account of the customer.

Connecting those records changes what the system can know. It doesn’t automatically change what the system will do. The decision process also needs to account for an unresolved refund and allow holding back a promotion as a valid outcome. Otherwise, you’ve given the system more information without changing the behavior it is rewarded for.

This is why customer context and objectives have to be designed together. Context explains what is happening. The objective and decision rules determine what should happen next. A return alone doesn’t mean all communication should stop. The customer may need a refund revision. The distinction between a useful service message and another promotion matters.

It has been revealed that A poorly written email is a content problem. A well-written email sent while the customer is waiting for their money is a decision problem. You can’t solve the second by getting better at the first.

Loyalty programs offer another version of the same problem. If success means more enrollments, a system may learn to recruit people with a discount. Enrollment rises. Whether those customers return without another discount is a different question.

Recent findings suggest that the useful questions take longer to answer. Are members coming back? Is their spending profitable after the cost of the incentives? Does the program change their behavior, or mostly reward purchases they would have made anyway?

In a recent development, answering those questions requires connecting loyalty activity with purchase and service history over time. It also requires a comparison that helps separate the program’s effect from behavior that was already likely. A larger membership count cannot tell you that on its own.

People are responsible for deciding what the system should optimize. Retention, margin and customer effort involve tradeoffs that leadership has to own. A model can help evaluate those tradeoffs. It can’t take responsibility for choosing them.

Industry observers note that the same is true of the limits on action. A useful starting question is: how hard would this be to undo? Holding a promotional message for review has different consequences from changing a price, issuing a credit or canceling a reservation. The consequences, the customer’s permissions and the reliability of the available context should determine what can run automatically and what needs approval.

Recent findings suggest that an open refund doesn’t need to become a manual review task every time. If the policy is clear, a rule can hold the promotion while service communication continues. Human review belongs where the context is ambiguous, the rules conflict or the consequences exceed the system’s authority. If the information needed to make that distinction is missing, the system needs a defined fallback rather than permission to guess.

Reviewers also need more than a confidence score. They need to see which customer records informed the recommendation, how current those records are, what the system is trying to achieve and which constraints apply. A confident recommendation based on stale or mismatched records is still a bad recommendation.

According to recent reports, overrides should become evidence. If people repeatedly stop the same kind of promotion, record why. The pattern may reveal missing service data, an identity problem or an objective that rewards the wrong behavior. Fixing that pattern is more valuable than asking a person to catch the same mistake indefinitely.

It has been revealed that teams can start with one decision rather than trying to redesign every customer interaction at once. Take a promotional send, identify the context it requires and define the conditions under which it should be held. Keep necessary service messages outside that suppression rule.

According to recent reports, then test whether the change helps. For eligible promotional messages, compare the existing approach with a policy that holds back under defined conditions. Track repeat purchases, retention, complaints and margin over a period that fits the buying cycle. Sends and clicks still help explain what happened, but they shouldn’t be the final verdict.

Recent findings suggest that the test may show that fewer promotions protect the relationship. It may show that a particular restriction is too broad. Either result is useful. Silence shouldn’t get a free pass any more than sending should. Both are decisions whose consequences can be measured.

Recent findings suggest that none of this removes the engineering work. Customer records have to resolve to the right person. Recent events have to reach the decision process in time to matter. Permissions have to constrain the action, and teams need a record of what happened and why. A better objective cannot compensate for missing context, just as better context cannot rescue the wrong objective.

The question for leaders is straightforward: what does your system count as a good decision? If the answer is a click, it may be doing its job while making the customer experience worse.

Trusted customer context gives people and AI a more dependable basis for deciding what to do. Clear objectives and controls determine how that understanding gets used. The result should be a system that can explain why a message is useful now, recognize when it isn’t and learn from what happens next.

Sometimes the smartest decision an AI system can make is to send nothing at all.

#23163. Breaking: How Rust Changed Me As A Developer

Breaking: How Rust Changed Me As A Developer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Startifact

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1.
  • In a recent development, I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now.
  • According to recent reports, what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty swiftly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.

In a recent development, I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.

According to recent reports, what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.

We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:.

The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak.

It has been revealed that but it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:.

Industry observers note that A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.

When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other.

Recent findings suggest that it turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error).

Recent findings suggest that any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.

Industry observers note that in an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:.

Recent findings suggest that the idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.

According to recent reports, this is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.

Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.

But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.

Or let's say you do want to add a newly introduced variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots!

In a recent development, or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.

In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.

According to recent reports, enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.

Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.

In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this:.

Sources indicate that rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].

There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.

What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.

It has been revealed that you could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just noted those don't actually exist.

Recent findings suggest that instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or Cat) during compile time.

Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.

In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is vital.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.

When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.

Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.

Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.

Recent findings suggest that subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.

Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.

In a recent development, subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.

It has been revealed that obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!

According to recent reports, subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.

Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.

Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.

In a recent development, here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.

It has been revealed that say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.

What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!

Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.

But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.

With serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:.

With clap, you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI.

Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just remarked Rust doesn't normally let you do that.

It has been revealed that how does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.

In a recent development, code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.

Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns.

Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.

Recent findings suggest that rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.

The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:.

Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.

It has been revealed that this feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.

Industry observers note that for circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.

It has been revealed that A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.

In a recent development, rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.

A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.

The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.

A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.

It has been revealed that in an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?

Sources indicate that iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.

fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.

interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.

the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.

Sources indicate that rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.

Industry observers note that I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software.

It has been revealed that rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.

When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.

But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access newly introduced qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.

In a recent development, sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.

Industry observers note that but it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore.

While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.

Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity.

Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning fresh ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it.

Recent findings suggest that rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10.

AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more notable to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.

If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.

You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true/false, or C's enum.

If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?

Recent findings suggest that does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.

Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.

It has been revealed that clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...

No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way.

AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has written a blog post that looks at vulnerabilities found by Anthropic's Project Glasswing since it released on April 7, and finds it wanting:.

Industry observers note that of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as "True Positives".

[...] AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Lazy Constants, Spring for Apache Pulsar, GlassFish, Hibernate, TomEE, Seed4J.

Nov 16, 2026 5 min read.

This week's Java roundup for November 9th, 2026, features news highlighting: Lazy Constants proposed to target for JDK 28; TornadoVM jitLLM 3.0; point releases of Seed4J; second release candidates of Spring AI and Spring Boot; first release candidates of Hibernate ORM and Hibernate Reactive; fourth milestone release of GlassFish; and the second milestone release of Apache TomEE.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case. The review is expected to conclude on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

In a recent development, build 24 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 23 that include fixes for various complications. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The second release candidate of Spring AI 2.1.0 delivers fresh features such as: a new DecisionModel API, anchored by the DecisionModel interface, that returns the probability of different outcomes instead of generated text based on yes/no answers, questions about text or a set of fields; and a new similaritySearch(float [], SearchRequest) method, added to the VectorStoreRetriever interface to complement the corresponding overloaded methods, to search with a user's embeddings in more vector stores. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The second release candidate of Spring Boot 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for reading the value defined in a X-Forwarded-Prefix HTTP header in a WebFlux application on Reactor Netty when the server.forward-headers-strategy property is set to native; and a database assigned to the spring.data.redis.database property is now properly applied to master/replica connections if a value is assigned to the spring.data.redis.masterreplica.nodes property. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

The Spring for Apache Pulsar team has announced that the project is moving as a subproject within Apache Pulsar at the Apache Software Foundation to "foster even deeper integration and collaboration with the broader Pulsar community." As stated in the blog post:.

Bringing this integration directly into the Apache Pulsar project allows the community to streamline development, accelerate feature support, and ensure long-term alignment with the evolution of Apache Pulsar.

Spring for Apache Pulsar 2.0.8, released in October 2026, was the final release under the auspices of the Spring ecosystem.

The fourth milestone release of GlassFish 9.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 specification with EclipseLink 6.0.0-M1; a move of the Sun Theme module out of the out of the external GlassFish Woodstock Components repository into its own module in GlassFish so that Sun Theme and the Admin Console can be modified together; and an upgrade to versions 1.2.0-M2 and 2.0.0-M1 of Eclipse JNoSQL. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Beehive Lab, makers of TornadoVM, has released version 3.0 of jitLLM, a JVM-native LLM inference and serving engine, delivers notable changes such as: 1.43 times faster startup with GraalVM Native Image; an up to 9.3 times faster prefill phase; and a more efficient reading of model weights by eliminating the copy from the mapped GGUF file into a Apple Metal buffer. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Hibernate ORM 8.0.0 ships with notable changes such as: an implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 and Jakarta Data 1.1.0-M4 specifications (the latter via Hibernate Data Repositories); and support for coordination of graph-based flushing that builds a dependency graph for pending entity and collection mutations. Further details on this release may be found in the what's new page.

The first release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 provide notable changes such as: the EXTENDED constant, defined in the Jakarta Persistence PessimisticLockScope enum class, now locks the collection tables as intended to align with the same functionality in Hibernate ORM; and an update to the VertxFactory interface to allow for adding observability without changing the functionality in using the DefaultVertxInstance class. These versions are compatible with Hibernate ORM 8.0.0.CR1. More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR1 and version 5.0.0.CR1.

Recent findings suggest that the second milestone release of Apache TomEE 11.0.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and latest features such as: resolutions to 38 CVEs; completion of their implementation of the Jakarta Authorization 3.0 specification; and TomEE Plume, the enterprise version, now ships the modular EclipseLink JPA artifact instead of the eclipselink Uber-Jar. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

According to recent reports, the release of JobRunr 9.0.4 ships with bug fixes and one fresh feature that improves build caching and security by moving to hardened Docker images. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

It has been revealed that the first rolling release of JReleaser 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT provides a upcoming feature in which the -a and -d short option flags, for their respective corresponding --assembly and --download long versions, were removed from the CLI due to the lack of short option flags for the --changelog and --announce flags. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Industry observers note that versions 2.4.0 and 2.3.0 of Seed4J, formerly known as JHipster Lite, deliver bug fixes, dependency upgrades and upcoming features such as: install Playwrite only on applications that execute the relevant Playwright component tests; and improved efficiency by creating one global Maven cache that is shared by the Seed4J build and every generated Maven application that replaces a Maven cache for each generated application. More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 2.4.0 and version 2.3.0.

The Quarkus team has introduced the Quarkus Resiliency Testing utility that allows developers to reproduce various failure scenarios and their respective responses while testing an application with the @QuarkusTest annotation. An example application using this latest utility may be found here.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • According to recent reports, this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

According to recent reports, this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

In a recent development, we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

Industry observers note that GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

Sources indicate that that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

According to recent reports, the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Sources indicate that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

According to recent reports, transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Recent findings suggest that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for upcoming architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

Industry observers note that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

According to recent reports, we also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

According to recent reports, our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

According to recent reports, A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

Sources indicate that the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

Sources indicate that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

Industry observers note that these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Industry observers note that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

It has been revealed that if you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an glitch with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

Isomorphic Labs confirmed on November 17, 2026 that it had raised $5 billion in Series C funding co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, giving the AI drug-discovery company upcoming capital to expand its design engine and move therapeutic candidates toward clinical trials.

It has been revealed that proceeds will fund further development of IsoDDE, the tech giant’s proprietary drug-design engine, expansion into newly introduced areas of biology, and global infrastructure for AI-led bioengineering. Isomorphic is also creating a partner ecosystem to study the mechanisms that drive disease. The company will also build translational and clinical-development infrastructure to move research toward patient testing and support candidates approaching trials.

Founder and CEO Demis Hassabis described the intended effect in the funding release: “This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients.”.

The fresh financing follows a $2.1 billion Series B declared on May 12, 2026, led by Thrive Capital. Alphabet and GV participated in that round alongside new investors MGX, Temasek, CapitalG and the UK Sovereign AI Fund. Thrive also led the $600 million first external round announced on March 31, 2025, which included GV and follow-on capital from Alphabet.

At the center of the business is IsoDDE, which the tech giant describes as a collection of AI simulation models built to handle different therapeutic areas and types of drugs. The system searches chemical space to design and refine molecules with drug-like properties, while proprietary agents navigate and reason through complex biology.

Isomorphic reports positive preclinical outcomes from wholly owned oncology and immunology programs and from partnered work, providing the basis for its planned move toward clinical trials.

It has been revealed that beyond its wholly owned programs, Isomorphic’s partnership portfolio includes Novartis, Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson. The Eli Lilly collaboration focuses on small-molecule therapeutics against undisclosed targets, while the multi-target Johnson & Johnson collaboration spans small molecules and biologics.

According to recent reports, novartis began working with Isomorphic in January 2024 on small molecules against three challenging targets. The companies expanded that work in February 2025, adding up to three additional research programs. Together, these programs give Isomorphic a portfolio that pairs firm-owned oncology and immunology work with partnered research spanning different drug modalities.

Industry observers note that the Series C gives Isomorphic the resources to develop its models and clinical-development infrastructure together. The central test is whether the reported preclinical progress translates into clinical evidence as candidates from its owned and partnered programs enter human trials.

  • Industry observers note that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

Recent findings suggest that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

Industry observers note that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

It has been revealed that this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this latest phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

According to recent reports, performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

In a recent development, when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Recent findings suggest that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Sources indicate that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Industry observers note that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
