Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Sources indicate that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Sources indicate that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern highlights up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

Industry observers note that A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

In a recent development, this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Recent findings suggest that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

In a recent development, the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a upcoming setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts stated 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

It has been revealed that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

According to recent reports, binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

It has been revealed that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This reveals it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

It has been revealed that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

In a recent development, that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Industry observers note that source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval indicates "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Recent findings suggest that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Sources indicate that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

It has been revealed that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cato Networks has unveiled AgentSense, a runtime security capability designed to stop harmful AI-agent actions before they execute.
  • Cato indicates AgentSense is integrated into its platform and will be included at no additional charge within Cato AI Usage licenses.
  • In a recent development, an enterprise agent may need to read emails, search documents, consult websites, and call tools to complete a task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cato Networks has unveiled AgentSense, a runtime security capability designed to stop harmful AI-agent actions before they execute. Developed by Cato AI Labs, the technology traces how untrusted content influences an agent’s behavior, addressing a risk that ordinary access permissions do not fully resolve: an agent can have legitimate credentials and still be manipulated into doing the wrong thing.

Cato indicates AgentSense is integrated into its platform and will be included at no additional charge within Cato AI Usage licenses. The announcement pairs the technology with an adversarial testing challenge offering $10,000 each to the first three eligible participants who successfully redirect a protected workflow into malicious actions.

In a recent development, an enterprise agent may need to read emails, search documents, consult websites, and call tools to complete a task. Each source expands the information it can use, but also creates an opportunity for outside text to influence its next step.

Recent findings suggest that indirect prompt injection exploits that boundary. Instead of issuing an instruction directly as the authorized user, an attacker hides one in material the agent encounters while working. A document, ticket, web page, or tool response can contain text that attempts to redirect the workflow, expose information, or trigger an unrelated action.

In a recent development, checking whether an agent can access an application remains crucial. It answers a different question from whether a particular action serves the task the user authorized. For example, an agent may be permitted to read business records without being authorized to send them to a destination suggested by a retrieved document.

AgentSense’s proposition is to evaluate that behavior during execution, with an opportunity to intervene before a sensitive action is carried out.

The confirmed Untrusted Influence Detection capability separates trusted instructions from untrusted content within an AI session and traces how the latter affects behavior and outputs. Cato says it blocks an action when it detects untrusted material steering the agent toward an unsafe step.

Industry observers note that the distinction is crucial because an attack does not have to look like a familiar malicious prompt. Cato describes AgentSense as assessing influence rather than relying on static classifiers or a catalog of previously observed attack patterns. That is intended to address fresh forms of indirect prompt injection as well as recognizable ones.

The release describes the technology as patented, but does not provide a patent identifier, detailed implementation, or independent effectiveness benchmark. Its claim of protection against previously unseen attacks should therefore be understood as the product’s intended security capability, rather than a guarantee that every prompt-injection attempt will be stopped.

Sources indicate that the operational question is whether a security layer has enough session and action context to distinguish using a document as evidence from treating that document as authority. AgentSense is aimed directly at that distinction.

It has been revealed that cato also describes AgentSense Drift Detection in forward-looking terms. The planned feature will evaluate whether an agent’s actions continue to serve the original task as a workflow progresses.

That complements influence detection without addressing exactly the same problem. Untrusted Influence Detection asks whether outside content is steering an action. Drift Detection is intended to ask whether the action still belongs to the objective, even if the individual step is technically permitted.

A workflow can gradually accumulate steps that no longer advance its purpose. Detecting that departure requires maintaining a view of the authorized objective across the session, rather than judging every tool call in isolation. The release does not specify a separate availability date for Drift Detection.

In a recent development, cato’s agentic AI security offering already describes controls for discovering agents and Model Context Protocol servers, profiling tool calls, and enforcing policies on agent interactions. Its broader platform combines networking, access, and security context.

The firm also separates security for employee AI use from protection for applications. Its AI Security for Applications offering describes runtime visibility, prompt and response inspection, and configurable protections for deployed AI applications. That provides context for AgentSense’s focus on the integrity of actions taken during a workflow.

In a recent development, in practice, controlling AI use involves several related decisions: which services an organization permits, which data may reach them, and what an agent may do with the information it encounters. AgentSense adds a behavioral claim to that stack—identifying when untrusted content is driving the action itself.

According to recent reports, cato’s EchoLeak research describes an attack chain in which externally supplied content could cause Microsoft 365 Copilot to expose information from its context. The significance for agent security is the transition from reading outside material to acting on instructions embedded in it.

Its CurXecute research examined a different outcome: prompt injection through external content could lead a coding agent to modify an MCP configuration and trigger command execution. Cato’s write-up says Cursor fixed that vulnerability in version 1.3. The example illustrates a failure mode; it should not be read as a claim that the patched issue remains open.

Both cases show why content provenance matters once an assistant can reach sensitive data or execution tools. An interaction that begins as information retrieval can become a security event when retrieved text changes the workflow’s control flow.

It has been revealed that the AgentSense Challenge invites the security community to plant instructions in a protected workflow and attempt to steer the agent away from the user’s intent. Cato says findings and participant feedback will inform further evaluation and improvement.

In a recent development, the first three eligible successful participants will each receive $10,000, according to the announcement. The supplied release does not include the final challenge URL or its detailed rules, so eligibility and testing boundaries will depend on the published program terms.

For enterprises expanding agent autonomy, AgentSense addresses a concrete need: preserving the connection between the task a user authorizes and the actions an AI system ultimately executes. The technology’s value will depend on how consistently it can enforce that boundary while allowing legitimate work to continue.

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • In a recent development, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

In a recent development, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

In a recent development, while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously noted by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

According to recent reports, importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

It has been revealed that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

According to recent reports, the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is key for voice agents and other interactive apps.

Recent findings suggest that for streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

Sources indicate that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

In a recent development, we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

According to recent reports, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Recent findings suggest that open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let consumers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

It has been revealed that human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Sources indicate that open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

According to recent reports, gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

Sources indicate that OVHcloud declared Olala, its first family of large language models, on November 17, 2026, starting with the compact Olala mini 7A1B. Industry observers note that an official launch presentation is scheduled for the OVHcloud AI Summit on November 19, 2026. The release package includes model weights, a pre-trained base model and compliance documentation for the AI Act, the European Union’s artificial-intelligence legislation.

According to recent reports, olala mini has a 7-billion-parameter architecture, but only 1 billion parameters are active for each request. Those active parameters are distributed across 256 experts per layer, so each request uses a fraction of the model rather than the full network. Its hybrid attention design combines Differential-TPA and Mamba-3 and uses BF16 format.

That structure is intended to increase speed and reduce memory demand. OVHcloud reports throughput of 160 tokens per second on an RTX A4500 and 50 tokens per second on a standard processor without a GPU. Its current context window—the amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can process in one sequence—is 32,000 tokens.

According to recent reports, olala mini was trained from scratch on three European public supercomputers: Jupiter, MeluXina and Jean Zay. The training infrastructure included GH200, A100 and H100 GPUs. OVHcloud describes the public support behind the project, equivalent to €7 million in computing hours, as decisive.

According to recent reports, the initiative also assembled the organization’s AI team and led to its Agentic Lab, OVHai LLM. That gives the project an organisational role beyond the first model: OVHcloud has established a dedicated group to continue developing the family rather than treating Olala mini as a one-off training exercise.

According to recent reports, qwant has already adopted Olala mini for its flash-answer feature. OVHcloud reports answers 20% faster and running costs divided by three compared with the model Qwant previously used, providing an early operational example of the deployment economics the manufacturer is pursuing.

OVHcloud’s roadmap calls for version 1.1 by the end of 2026, extending the context window to 128,000 tokens and improving mathematical reasoning. Version 2.0 is planned to exceed 100 billion parameters, with OVHai LLM developing models specialised in business agentic AI, cloud DevOps and cybersecurity, including defensive and offensive uses.

Later versions are intended to move the family into OVHcloud’s products and operational tools. Olala is eventually expected to power OVHai Workspace, whose encrypted version will require models capable of running locally on a workstation. The DevOps work includes versions for developers, architects and operations teams responsible for round-the-clock service continuity.

Chief executive Octave Klaba said OVHcloud needs to create models for its own internal requirements as well as customer needs. “We cannot simply rely on the generosity of certain labs to share their LLMs as open source in the years to come,” he said. Klaba said training expertise has become widely accessible and costs have fallen by a factor of 20 in three years, presenting those changes as a route to profitable model development.

Olala therefore gives OVHcloud both a compact model and an in-house development path. The central question is whether OVHai LLM can carry the efficiency and deployment gains reported for this first model into the larger-context release and the much bigger, specialised systems laid out in its roadmap.

Industry News: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates newly introduced tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

In a recent development, the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Industry observers note that realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

According to recent reports, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

In a recent development, consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

It has been revealed that completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

It has been revealed that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

It has been revealed that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into upcoming executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

According to recent reports, we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create newly introduced tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Recent findings suggest that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a latest target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

According to recent reports, to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Sources indicate that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

According to recent reports, generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Sources indicate that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

In a recent development, failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

Industry observers note that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

It has been revealed that the controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

According to recent reports, the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

In a recent development, after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Sources indicate that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We proposal to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

Industry observers note that we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I must unfortunately announce that Redict is officially deprecated, and Redict 7.3.6 is the final release.
  • I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • Recent findings suggest that we recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I must unfortunately announce that Redict is officially deprecated, and Redict 7.3.6 is the final release.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project’s success, and Redis’s return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

Switching to valkey is straightforward: if you install from your package manager, simply install valkey and move your config file:.

If you use containers, simply pull the valkey container instead and ensure that it runs with the appropriate config file.

Thanks to everyone who has contributed to Redict, endorsed the fork as the future of Redis, and switched to it on their own machines. We had a good run :).

Oran Moyal, Co-Founder and CTO of Ocean Security – Interview Series

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, oran Moyal is Co-Founder and CTO of Ocean Security, where he develops agentic AI for investigating sophisticated email threats.
  • Ocean Security builds an agentic email security platform designed to investigate targeted phishing, business email compromise, and financial fraud.
  • Before co-founding Ocean in 2024, you spent years working in cybersecurity research and development, including roles in the Israel Defense Forces and at VisibleRisk / Microsoft Security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, oran Moyal is Co-Founder and CTO of Ocean Security, where he develops agentic AI for investigating sophisticated email threats. His background spans cybersecurity research and development, offensive social engineering, and enterprise security. He co-founded Ocean in 2024 with Shay Shwartz, drawing on their experience analyzing how attackers exploit trusted communication and how security systems can respond to increasingly targeted threats.

Ocean Security builds an agentic email security platform designed to investigate targeted phishing, business email compromise, and financial fraud. Its specialized AI agents analyze communication context and sender intent to help security teams identify threats within seemingly legitimate business interactions. In this interview, Moyal discusses what makes an organization AI-native, how to redesign workflows around agents, and why clear requirements, independent validation, enforced permissions, and human judgment remain central to effective automation.

Before co-founding Ocean in 2024, you spent years working in cybersecurity research and development, including roles in the Israel Defense Forces and at VisibleRisk / Microsoft Security. What experiences led you to launch Ocean, and how did the emergence of AI influence your vision for the company from the outset?

A targeted spear phishing campaign used to take a dedicated team and weeks of manual research and preparation. When generative AI arrived, we realized that every employee in every enterprise is now subject to a devastating nation-state-level phishing attack. Overnight, a $20 subscription gave every attacker nation-state capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that shay and I have deep social engineering expertise from the offensive side, and we’ve both built and scaled enterprise security companies, so we knew legacy tools couldn’t keep up. They look for rule violations and anomalies, but these attacks live inside normal business communication: real threads, trusted accounts and legitimate services. Nothing looks abnormal. So, in 2024 we started Ocean to help enterprises adapt to this new threat with AI-driven email security that analyzes context and sender intent in real time, much like a human investigator would, before a compromise occurs.

Industry observers note that many organizations describe themselves as “AI-native” simply because they’ve adopted AI tools or automated certain processes. In your view, what fundamentally distinguishes a truly AI-native organization from one that has simply integrated AI into its existing operations?

Many companies call themselves AI-native because they’ve bought AI tools. That’s technology adoption. Being AI-native changes how the tech giant handles everyday work and how it solves bottlenecks.

According to recent reports, it starts with how leaders respond to a bottleneck. The traditional reflex is “This takes too much time; let’s hire someone to handle it.” An AI-native organization first asks, “How can AI speed up this entire function?” Repeat that question across every team, and the whole organization starts operating differently.

Sources indicate that real AI-native transformation is organizational, not technical. If you speed up one department, the bottleneck just moves to the next one, and the firm ends up moving at the pace of its slowest function. AI-native organizations change together, so information flows faster, feedback loops get shorter and teams work as one connected system.

According to recent reports, in this model, the value of people shifts. As AI takes on more of the work, the scarce skills are setting clear direction, defining intent and applying judgment. People and agents work side by side. AI handles more of the execution, and people decide what is worth building and why.

The goal is for every team to do more with the same resources, move faster and work better together, without compromising quality.

You’ve argued that AI-driven productivity gains can swiftly disappear when the underlying workflows are inefficient. What are the most common operational bottlenecks that prevent companies from realizing the full benefits of AI, and how should leaders approach redesigning these workflows?

According to recent reports, speeding up individual tasks doesn’t automatically speed up the organization. If processes, dependencies and communication between teams stay the same, most of the productivity AI creates gets lost along the way.

The most common bottlenecks aren’t technical. They’re unclear requirements that cause repeated rework, slow handoffs between teams and work that sits waiting for approvals. AI makes each step faster, but the time is lost between the steps.

Recent findings suggest that leaders should start by measuring where time actually goes, because the real bottleneck is often not the one everyone assumes. Then redesign the workflow from start to finish, fixing the handoffs, definitions and feedback loops rather than only individual tasks. Finally, connect every AI effort to the KPIs teams already own.

It has been revealed that most importantly, leaders need to change the mindset. Automation and acceleration should become the default. Instead of accepting existing processes, teams should keep challenging how things are done so they can move faster and increase their impact without compromising quality.

Recent findings suggest that one of the principles you emphasize is the importance of clearly defined requirements before introducing AI agents into a workflow. How should organizations rethink the way they define tasks, communicate expectations, and establish success criteria when AI agents are responsible for executing significant portions of the work?

When AI agents do a large part of the work, organizations need to rethink how they communicate and define tasks. A vague request doesn’t stop an agent. It guesses, and every wrong guess leads to more rework.

I think about it in three layers:.

Clear tasks, goals and context. The agent needs to understand what needs to be done, why it matters and the context around it. Before the work starts, it should be able to ask about anything unclear, so gaps are resolved upfront instead of discovered halfway through.

Self-validation. Success criteria should be defined in advance, in a way the agent can check on its own. In software, for example, an agent should be able to run the code, test that it works as intended and confirm that it passes the tests before anyone reviews it.

According to recent reports, humans as the final layer. People should receive a result the agent has already refined over several iterations against the agreed criteria. Their role is to apply judgment, not to fix basic mistakes.

The better the definition, the less human time each result needs.

According to recent reports, you advocate enabling AI agents to validate their own work before it reaches human reviewers. What does an effective AI-driven validation process look like in practice, and how can organizations ensure that automated quality checks don’t simply reinforce the same mistakes made during execution?

It has been revealed that an effective validation process tests the work the way it will actually be used. The agent should run the real system from start to finish, confirm the result matches the success criteria and fix what fails before anything reaches a person.

To keep validation from repeating the agent’s own mistakes, a few principles matter:.

Separate the criteria from the execution. People should define what success looks like before the work starts. If an agent decides what “done” means, it will grade its own homework.

Industry observers note that set hard guardrails. Not every check should depend on an agent’s judgment. Some must be fixed, deterministic tests that verify specific parameters, standards and policies. These give the agent clear boundaries it can’t reason its way around.

Use an independent reviewer. A second agent, with fresh context and no stake in the original approach, catches errors the first one misses.

Show evidence, not just a verdict. Test results, screenshots and recordings let people see what happened instead of trusting a “pass.”.

Human attention then goes where the risk is highest. The goal isn’t to remove people from the process. It’s to make sure their time goes to judgment, not mechanical checks.

Industry observers note that traditional organizations often rely on multiple layers of management, approvals, and handoffs between teams. How does an AI-native operating model change the way engineering, product, security, and business teams collaborate, and what happens to traditional roles and responsibilities as agents take on more of the execution?

AI lets every person and every team produce more. But if handoffs, approvals and coordination stay the same, that extra output just piles up waiting for the next step. The organization doesn’t move faster. It creates newly introduced bottlenecks. An AI-native operating model has to redesign how teams work together, not only how each team works.

That starts with how information moves. More of it should flow through automation, so meetings are saved for decisions rather than updates. When insights from the field reach product directly, decisions become faster and more accurate, and that carries through to clearer definitions and better execution.

Approvals need the same rethinking, and this is the hardest part, because it means changing what the organization treats as normal. Approvals still matter, but they shouldn’t treat every change the same way. For example, adding a risk assessment to a specific approval process can reduce manual approvals for low-risk work while keeping human review where it counts. That’s just one way to speed up a process without giving up control.

It has been revealed that roles are being redefined as well. As agents take on more of the execution, people move from owning tasks to owning outcomes. They need to understand the full context, challenge assumptions and step beyond their traditional boundaries. The organizations that win will be the ones that redesign how people work together, not only the ones that add the most AI.

Recent findings suggest that ocean itself uses specialized AI agents to investigate sophisticated email threats. How has your experience developing agentic AI for cybersecurity influenced the way you deploy AI internally, and are there lessons from building autonomous security systems that apply to managing an AI-native organization?

Building autonomous agents for email security shaped how we use AI internally in two ways.

The first lesson is that agents perform only as well as their understanding of context. A security agent makes better decisions when it understands the organization it protects. The same is true internally. To get good results from agents, we need to give them a real understanding of how the organization works, what each task is for and how it connects to the bigger picture.

It has been revealed that the second is that agents need continuous evaluation. In production, we constantly evaluate how our agents perform, where they fail and which tools or data they’re missing. Internally, we apply the same approach. We need a dedicated place to test, train and get feedback on agents. Without it, it’s hard to tell whether an agent is improving or what it needs next.

Running an AI-native organization is a lot like building an autonomous security system: give agents deep context, keep evaluating how they perform, and keep people in the loop where judgment counts.

According to recent reports, as organizations give AI agents greater autonomy, concerns arise around accountability, security, and unintended consequences. Drawing on your cybersecurity background, how should companies establish guardrails that allow agents to operate independently without compromising security or losing meaningful human oversight?

In a recent development, autonomy is where agents are heading, and organizations should get there step by step. Start where the impact is well understood, prove the value and then expand.

Real guardrails aren’t instructions. Telling an agent “don’t do this” isn’t a security control. Guardrails need to be enforced: strict limits on what the agent can access, verification that it can’t reach anything outside its scope, and continuous monitoring that blocks actions nobody planned for. Like any other part of the system, they should be tested and validated regularly.

Sources indicate that accountability starts with the operator. The person running an agent defines its boundaries: what it can do on its own, what needs approval and where it can’t go. Take an agent that responds to email threats. It can quarantine suspicious messages on its own, rapidly and reliably. For actions with wider impact, such as blocking a sender across the entire organization, the operator may start with a review step. As the agent’s track record grows, those boundaries can expand with confidence. Clear guardrails are what make greater autonomy possible.

This matters even more because attackers are increasingly targeting AI agents. The business wants to move faster, but security teams still don’t have a clear playbook for protecting agents. That’s why the foundation has to be enforced permissions and constant monitoring.

Many companies measure AI adoption through time saved, tasks automated, or employee productivity. What metrics do you believe actually demonstrate whether an AI-native operating model is delivering sustainable business value, particularly when accounting for rework, quality, and coordination costs?

Time saved is an important metric, and it’s often the first clear sign that AI is creating value. But it demonstrates its full impact when it’s paired with metrics that show what the organization does with that time, and whether the gains hold up over the long term.

Quality. Faster is only better if quality holds or improves. Track rework, defects and how often results need to be corrected after delivery. When speed and quality improve together, the gains are real and lasting.

According to recent reports, business expansion. The real value of an AI-native organization is what the time it saves makes possible. We measure how many new capabilities and initiatives we take on without adding headcount.

End-to-end speed. How long an agent takes to develop a feature is one part of the picture. The real measure is the full process, including every handoff, from the moment we decide to prioritize something to the moment it’s live in the product. That’s how fast we actually run, and it shows the coordination costs that task-level metrics miss. In security, end-to-end speed is critical. Attackers are already using AI agents, so the time it takes to detect and respond to a threat has to keep shrinking.

Recent findings suggest that time saved shows that AI is working. These metrics show it’s building lasting value for the business.

You’ve suggested that smaller, more agile technology companies can gain a meaningful competitive advantage by redesigning their operations around AI. What advantages do AI-native startups have over established incumbents, and how do you envision the structure of successful technology companies evolving over the next three to five years?

It has been revealed that AI-native startups have a structural advantage. They can build workflows, technology and teams around AI agents from day one, while incumbents must deal with decades of legacy infrastructure and organizational complexity. The bigger gap isn’t technical. Everyone has access to the same AI tools. The advantage belongs to companies that can redesign how they work, without layers of approvals, handoffs and fixed roles to unwind first.

Over the next three to five years, I believe successful technology companies will move beyond basic AI automation toward agentic operating models, where specialized AI agents execute entire workflows. Human teams won’t disappear, but people will spend less time executing tasks by hand and more time providing context, setting guardrails and directing outcomes. The result will be leaner organizations that can scale faster, operate more efficiently and compete with companies many times their size.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Scaling LLM-Based Ranking Systems for Latency-Critical Search & Recommendation Workloads.

Sources indicate that sundara Raman Ramachandran shares how LinkedIn productionizes LLM ranking under strict P99 latency SLAs. He discusses distilling a 7B model down to 400M parameters, compressing job contexts into single-token embeddings for a 10x throughput leap, and eliminating hidden system bottlenecks - from custom flash attention masks to Python GIL workarounds, gc.freeze, and non-blocking CUDA memory copies.

Sundara Raman Ramachandran is a Lead Engineer on LinkedIn’s LLM Inference team, where he plays a key role in designing and scaling the infrastructure powering LLM-based ranking systems for search and recommendation. His work centers on building latency-critical, high-throughput LLM serving platforms that operate reliably at global scale.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Sundara Raman Ramachandran: I'm Sundara. I'm a tech lead at LinkedIn. My current focus is on LLM inference and using LLMs for ranking and recommendation workloads. I'm also an open-source contributor in SGLang where I have primarily contributed to the scoring API where we use LLMs for ranking. I have close to 10 years of industry experience. I have worked with Microsoft in different products like Microsoft Office and Azure. Today I'm going to talk about how we scale the LLM based ranking systems at LinkedIn, what were the challenges we encountered, and what are some learnings and takeaways you can take from the talk.

I hope all of you would have used LinkedIn at some point, that you might have used it for searching for some job or you're looking for someone in a network. Earlier we used to search based on specific keywords, and there were specific search filters that you put when you're entering any search query. Nowadays we are moving into more of a natural language to specify our intent. In LinkedIn's use case, you might be searching for a job where you enter, find me design roles in the entertainment industry.

Industry observers note that or you're searching for someone in your network where the search query could be, who in my network can help me file a patent for my business? All these are raw natural language texts which are complex to understand. If you think about this, this is where LLMs can be really powerful. They help us understand the user intent and then help us provide them better results. Search and ranking at LinkedIn scale is already a complex enough problem, and if you bring LLMs into the mix, it makes it even harder. For engineers like me, it's a really fun problem to solve.

Industry observers note that let's look at the high-level architecture of how these things work end-to-end. It all starts with a search query where you have the find me design roles in the entertainment industry, and the search query goes through the first layer called query understanding layer. This is where we help figure out what the user intent is, what they're actually looking for. Then comes the retrieval layer. LinkedIn has millions of jobs posted in this platform. The job of the retrieval layer is to figure out the top-K most relevant jobs for your search query. Then all these results go to the ranker layer, which ultimately decides the order in which we want to show the results to you guys. In this talk, I'm going to quickly give an overview of the query understanding and the retrieval layer to add more context to the overall talk. My specific talk is going to be focused on the ranking layer.

Let's look at the query understanding layer first. The goal of the query understanding layer is to turn the raw, ambiguous natural language text that the user has entered and convert that into more of a structured, normalized format, which the further systems can understand. Let's take this example where we have a member who's a software engineer in the Bay Area with 5 years of experience. The search query they have entered is, find software engineer jobs near my location. We take this query and then the first step here is the query planner, which identifies the search criteria here. In this case, it's a job title and location, and figures out a initiative on how to execute it. The next comes the query tagger. This step enriches the query with more rich information, which we can pull from the member profile, like what is their job title, what is their location, and also some search filters they might have in their LinkedIn.

Sources indicate that next comes the query rewriter, which is essentially the crucial piece here. If you look at a search query, we have something like a self-referencing, ambiguous text there, find me software engineer job near my location. Someone has to go and really understand what the user location is. That's where the query rewriter comes into play. It's going to replace the near my location with Bay Area, which is the user location. All of this gets packaged into a nice format, normalized enough, and then passed on to the retrieval layer.

Now when we move on to the retrieval layer, the goal here is for the user query, we have to find the top-K semantically relevant jobs. We have millions of jobs posted out there. We cannot go take every job and rank them. That's where the input starts with the query understanding layer output, and we take that and convert that into a query embedding. We then do a vector search with the embedding and do a KNN search on the index, which was pre-built using all the pre-computed embeddings from the jobs out there. From this step, we get the top-K most semantically relevant jobs for the search query. In this step, we primarily focus on optimizing for recall rather than precision. What we exactly mean by that is we would rather have a few extra candidates out of the retrieval layer than discarding something which is highly relevant.

The output from the retrieval layer then is passed on to the ranking layer. As mentioned about previously, this is where we figure out what order we want to show the results to the user. We want to show the highly relevant one as the first item. If you haven't already guessed, in LinkedIn right now, we are employing LLMs to do this job for us. As with any LLM, the first step is to provide enough context for the LLM to make the right decision. That's where the output from the previous two layers, the query understanding and the retrieval layer becomes the context for this LLM. Then comes the system prompt. You have to build the prompt. You have to tell the LLM to do a specific job. You'll be surprised what we have in production. It goes by this, like we prompt the LLM, given a search query and given the member profile description and a job, can you output yes or no if the job matches the query?

Sources indicate that it's literally that. That's what we really have in production. At the end of this, we take the probabilities of model predicting yes or no token, and use that to compute the final scores. We do this for all the candidates provided by the retrieval layer, and then finally do some business logic to show what is the first result we want to show to you.

Recent findings suggest that when you're operating systems at this scale and you're serving billions of members out there, you want to optimize all the layers underneath. That's where we have three main levels. Before going to that, I'm going to specify why LLM ranking is a very different problem. Usually, when we think about LLMs, we associate with chatbot text generation. Ranking is a very different problem all together. If you look at the generative LLM workloads, you have a prompt which you give to the LLM and it goes through a phase called prefill phase. Prefill phase is the one that the LLM understands the context you have given to it. Next comes the decode phase, and we call it decode loop here because we are generating text token by token. It goes through several steps like sampling, next token prediction. You want to get the probabilities of all the token and the vocabulary and figure out what is the token you want to output to the user, which ultimately gives you the generated text token by token.

In a recent development, the latency here scales with the number of output tokens required. If you take a ranking use case, let's take the job ranking scenario. We talked about the query here is software engineer jobs in Bay Area, and the system prompt is simple, like output yes or no based on a job match. The list of candidates or the list of items to be ranked here is the job description. The main difference here, let's say we want to rank 50 items, we are constructing 50 prompts to the LLM for each item. You'll have a query item 1, query item 2, like that, 50 items. All of this goes through a single batched prefill phase. Another vital difference here is all of this share a common long shared prefix in terms of the query, in terms of the system prompt, and all other context you feed to the LLM.

Recent findings suggest that these are shared among all the jobs you want to rank. The third one here is there is not necessarily a decode phase. We are not generating any text per se. All we need is the final probabilities of the yes or no token. The major challenges when serving a system like this is we are dealing with strict P99 latency SLAs. Imagine you go to LinkedIn and search something and we take 10 seconds to show the result. That is not a good experience. We are also dealing with high concurrency where it's not enough if we just show one job or one person in a network, we have to show a bunch of candidates, usually in the hundreds. These challenges require us to optimize on all possible trends. That's where these three come into play. In an LLM system, we have the model, we have the context, and we have the inference.

Whenever you're working with these kinds of systems, you want to make the model as small as possible and you want to make the context as short as possible, because token here is the currency. Inference, you have to make it as efficient as possible. In the rest of the talk, I'm going to dive deep into each of these sections where I'm going to share what we did, what worked for us, and what are some learnings that you could take away from us.

Let's start with the model optimizations. The goal is simple. Like you have a model, you want to make it as small as possible. What are the techniques we can employ for this? The first thing we did is something called multi-teacher distillation. We started with the larger model, around 7-billion parameter size. This model is really good in understanding the context. It can understand the product policies and it can understand the relevance between the query and item, but it was never intended to be deployed in production. The whole purpose of this teacher model or the larger model is to provide high quality training signals. We then transfer this knowledge into two separate smaller teacher models by a process called knowledge distillation. We have two models which are optimized for separate metrics, one for relevance, another for engagement. These are metrics in ranking and recommendation workloads. The relevance here basically denotes how relevant is the search result for the query.

The engagement here basically specifies, if I show this result to the user, how likely it is to drive engagement, whether the user will click, whether the user will read, and all those things. Now we have two smaller teacher models, we call it, which is optimized on these two metrics. We then use this and then train another small model, SLM ranker is what we call it, small language model, which learns the objectives from both of these teacher models. We essentially started with a larger 7 billion model and we were able to knowledge distill all this in a multi-step, in a multi-teacher way, and then compress all the context into the smaller model. You will have some quality loss, but it should be acceptable for the business use case you're solving. We didn't stop there. We looked into how to make this model even smaller. That's where a technique called pruning comes into play.

Sources indicate that it's essentially, you take the model and you do some trial and error and figure out, can I remove some layers? Can I remove some MLP layers or any attention heads? Then see if there is an acceptable quality loss that you can still serve. Obviously, pruning doesn't come for free. Whenever you're removing something from the model, there will be some quality loss. That's why we have to again re-distill, re-train and fine-tune the model so that the loss is within the acceptable range. Just to recall the model optimizations, we started with the 7 billion larger model with the multi-teacher distillation. We got it to 0.6B. We took the 0.6B and then removed some layers and finally got this in the size of 400 million parameters. Now the model is super small that we can now already serve this in production.

Industry observers note that next, I want to talk about the context optimization. If we take the job ranking scenario and a particular job description can easily be 2000 tokens. When you want to serve a ranking request, so you have a request and you have 100 jobs you want to rank. This could easily be 100 into 2000, like 200K tokens that you want to process in one shot.
