Industry News: AI Compute in 2027: The Cost of Inference Will Reshape the Data Center

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A data center can be full of expensive accelerators and still be short of useful capacity.
  • According to recent reports, in 2027, more of the compute contest will be fought over what each installed system can deliver under the conditions customers actually require.
  • The baseline is already moving quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A data center can be full of expensive accelerators and still be short of useful capacity. Some chips are waiting for memory. Others are serving requests that miss their latency target. A benchmark may look excellent while the service bill keeps climbing. Owning the hardware is only the beginning of the economic problem.

According to recent reports, in 2027, more of the compute contest will be fought over what each installed system can deliver under the conditions customers actually require. That shifts attention toward serving software, workload placement and the cost of an acceptable answer.

The baseline is already moving quickly. MLPerf Inference v6.1, released in September 2026, added end-to-end retrieval-augmented generation and an edge agentic workload. It also described the transition toward an API-centric Endpoints suite. This is evidence that benchmark designers are adapting to multi-stage workloads, not evidence that every AI application can be represented by a single benchmark score.

Meanwhile, the IEA’s 2026 energy analysis describes a tension between efficiency gains per task and the growth of more demanding applications. It reports rising data-center electricity use and stresses the uncertainty created by changing workloads. The inference I draw is that falling unit costs will intensify competition over system design while leaving power and memory as consequential constraints. They will not automatically make the total infrastructure bill fall.

The next capacity increase may arrive as a software deployment. Scheduling, memory management and execution kernels can change how much work an installed accelerator completes without changing the chip itself. I expect a reproducible 2027 result showing at least 30% more throughput within the latency target on the fixed hardware and model defined here. The interesting business consequence is additional usable capacity from a purchase the operator has already made.

The economic attraction is straightforward. Hardware that is already installed has a capacity cost whether its scheduler uses it efficiently or not. Better batching, kernel execution, memory allocation, and request routing can raise the amount of useful output without adding accelerators. That is especially valuable where a newly introduced rack would also require more power, cooling, or network capacity.

It has been revealed that the original PagedAttention research demonstrates why memory management belongs in the performance discussion: inefficient handling of the key-value cache can waste capacity and limit batching. Its historical results should not be carried forward as a universal speedup on current systems. They establish the mechanism, rather than the size of the next gain.

Recent findings suggest that there is contemporary evidence of continuing headroom. In its v6.1 submission analysis, AMD reports higher throughput on the same MI355X hardware between benchmark rounds, including a 38% Server improvement on its specified GPT-OSS-120B configuration. That vendor comparison concerns a different model from my forecast target. It supports the proposition that software maturity still matters; it does not establish that a 30% gain on Llama 3.1 8B is guaranteed.

Sources indicate that the fixed workload in this prediction is deliberate. A claim that one system produces more tokens after switching to a smaller model, lower quality, or a looser latency target tells a different economic story. The test needs to hold those choices still. AMD’s published reproduction recipes provide a useful example of exposing software and configuration details, even though vendor-provided recipes still require independent scrutiny.

Look for serving benchmarks that improve throughput on hardware already installed while holding the model, answer quality, and response-time requirements steady. Published configurations and latency distributions will make those gains easier to assess. Results achieved through smaller models, lower precision without quality checks, or relaxed latency targets would support a different claim.

Infrastructure buyers should measure the headroom in their current serving stack before committing to more accelerators. Compare the cost of software upgrades, tuning, and operational support with the capacity they could unlock. Expansion decisions should use accepted requests under the application's service targets, so a higher headline token rate does not conceal a poorer customer experience.

Recent findings suggest that reading a long prompt and generating an answer ask different things of a serving system. Putting both jobs on the same hardware is convenient, but convenience can leave expensive resources poorly matched to the work. In 2027, named operators will show where separating those stages produces a substantial gain in requests served per accelerator-hour. The result will depend on traffic shape; a better architecture for one service can be an unnecessary complication for another.

Sources indicate that prefill processes the incoming context. Decoding generates the answer token by token. Their resource demands and latency objectives differ, which means a shared pool can create interference or force overprovisioning. Splitting the phases allows separate allocation, but adds the cost of moving state between them.

In a recent development, distServe formalized that trade-off around goodput: work completed within the service’s latency constraints. Its reported improvements came from particular evaluated workloads and conditions. They should not be read as a general multiplier for every production cluster. Network topology, context length, output length, and traffic variation determine whether separation pays for itself.

Recent findings suggest that by 2026, this is more than a research proposal. NVIDIA Dynamo includes a planner, cache-aware routing, and transfer components for distributed inference. NVIDIA’s analysis of multimodal disaggregation is useful partly because it identifies conditions where benefits shrink or a topology underperforms. A supplier describing the losing conditions gives buyers a more useful starting point than a single maximum speedup.

My forecast is conditional on the right workloads reaching sufficient scale. Long prompts and uneven demand can create enough scheduling friction to justify a more complex serving architecture. Small, steady workloads may be served more economically by keeping the system simple. Separating stages is therefore a capacity-management decision, with software and operational costs that must be earned back.

Industry observers note that watch for operators publishing results from real request mixes, including long prompts, variable demand, and the cost of moving state between inference stages. Gains should remain visible after all reserved accelerators and transfer overhead are included. Deployments that add complexity without improving useful work per unit of capacity would narrow the case for disaggregation.

Treat prefill–decode separation as an architecture choice to validate against your traffic. Teams should model the extra networking, scheduling, and operating demands before adopting it. Large, uneven workloads may justify that effort; smaller services should require evidence that the additional components earn back their cost under normal operating conditions.

It has been revealed that A cheaper accelerator is a bargain only if the finished answer is acceptable and arrives in time. That leaves room for alternatives to NVIDIA on selected workloads, even while software maturity and availability remain formidable advantages for the incumbent. I expect independent 2027 comparisons to demonstrate a meaningful cost advantage across two different alternative families. The comparison has to survive the migration and operating details that disappear from a chip specification sheet.

This is a prediction about specific operating points, not a prediction of a wholesale platform replacement. A serving stack can be attractive for one model and traffic pattern while being unsuitable for another. Porting effort, operator familiarity, supported kernels, and the availability of useful instances can outweigh a favorable hardware specification.

According to recent reports, several suppliers already offer substantial alternatives. Google’s Ironwood documentation specifies high-bandwidth memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnect characteristics. AWS’s Trainium3 availability announcement describes a platform designed for dense and expert-parallel workloads. AMD’s MLPerf submissions establish standardized workload participation. None of these sources, by itself, proves the price advantage in my forecast.

The comparison becomes economically meaningful only after the workload is fixed. If an accelerator requires more hosts, a different parallelism scheme, or longer reservation commitments, those costs belong in the denominator. An advertised price that cannot be purchased in the tested region should not determine the result. The same applies to unused reserved capacity and a favorable benchmark assembled from hardware that customers cannot actually obtain.

I assign moderate confidence because technical competitiveness and transparent economics are separate hurdles. The test may be achievable while its cost details remain commercially private. It is also possible for a competing accelerator to win on throughput while losing on operational simplicity. A complete decision should show recurring infrastructure expense and one-time migration effort separately.

According to recent reports, look for comparisons run by organizations other than the winning chip supplier, using purchasable capacity and equivalent quality and latency requirements. The decisive evidence will include host, networking, idle capacity, and migration assumptions. A compelling accelerator specification without a reproducible serving-cost comparison would leave the economic prediction unproven.

Recent findings suggest that build hardware evaluations around a representative model and traffic trace, then price the complete deployment. Keep recurring operating savings separate from porting, retraining staff, and maintaining another software stack. An alternative accelerator can be attractive for a specific service without becoming the right platform for every workload the business runs.

Sources indicate that an agent can consume energy while thinking, calling tools, retrying and eventually failing. Measuring one inference step misses that story. By the end of 2027, I expect the MLPerf lineage of agentic benchmarks to put measured system energy beside successfully completed work. That would give operators a better denominator for a difficult question: how much infrastructure does this service consume to produce something the customer can actually use?

An agent can make repeated model calls, revisit a long context, invoke tools, and retry failed steps. A per-token energy figure captures only part of the cost of that behavior. The relevant unit for a multi-step workload is the completed task, with a declared boundary around the infrastructure being measured.

The v6.1 announcement already describes growing conversational history in agentic inference, an edge agentic test, and work toward datacenter agentic benchmarking. The forecast therefore concerns a further measurement requirement, rather than the debut of agentic benchmarks. I expect pressure to connect those workloads to system energy as inference buyers confront power constraints.

In a recent development, the IEA’s 2026 assessment provides the broader reason to care: the relationship between efficiency and total demand depends on uptake and workload complexity. A short-answer query and a long-running agent cannot be assigned the same representative energy cost. Likewise, an efficient individual accelerator does not establish an efficient complete workflow.

This prediction has the lowest confidence in the article because measurement standards take coordination. Tool services may run outside the measured system. A benchmark may choose reproducibility over realism, or report power without an end-to-end task success gate. Those can be defensible design decisions, but they would not satisfy this particular forecast.

Sources indicate that watch for agentic benchmark reports that put measured energy beside completed tasks and explain which components are inside the measurement boundary. Repeated model calls, retries, and unsuccessful attempts should remain visible. Reporting only accelerator power or energy per token would leave buyers with an incomplete picture of the cost of a multi-step agent.

Capacity and sustainability teams should agree on a useful unit of work before comparing energy figures. Track how many tasks succeed, the resources consumed by failed attempts, and the infrastructure excluded from the estimate. That accounting can help teams decide whether a more capable agent also makes efficient use of their available power and compute budgets.

Industry observers note that the scarce resource will be capacity that meets the service requirement at an acceptable cost. Faster chips will matter, but so will a scheduler that wastes less, a memory layout that fits the workload and a measurement that counts failures honestly. The next data-center advantage may be less visible than a latest rack—and more consequential to the bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Recent findings suggest that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

It has been revealed that we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

Industry observers note that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Recent findings suggest that add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

According to recent reports, boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Industry observers note that for edits, each region states where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

In a recent development, everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

According to recent reports, A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

According to recent reports, let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

According to recent reports, so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

Recent findings suggest that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

Sources indicate that at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

It has been revealed that in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

Sources indicate that the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Industry observers note that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

In a recent development, text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

In a recent development, FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Industry observers note that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

In a recent development, the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are latest to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

Sources indicate that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo is bringing AI-assisted banking, payroll, tax preparation, and credit into a more connected platform for small businesses.
  • In a recent development, the expansion comes as Novo’s own customers spend more on AI.
  • Industry observers note that for Novo, the product opportunity is to make financial software respond more like an assistant that understands the business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo is bringing AI-assisted banking, payroll, tax preparation, and credit into a more connected platform for small businesses. The November 17 launch pairs natural-language access to financial information with transaction labeling and analytics, aiming to reduce the administrative work owners handle across separate applications.

In a recent development, the expansion comes as Novo’s own customers spend more on AI. In an analysis of anonymized, aggregated data from its customer base, the company found that monthly spending on a group of AI tools increased 493% between November 2024 and June 2026. The number of businesses paying for those tools rose 145% over the same period.

Industry observers note that for Novo, the product opportunity is to make financial software respond more like an assistant that understands the business. But the details of its rollout also show where that assistance stops: the banking agent requires approval for actions, the developer API is in closed beta, and filing for the 2026 tax year opens in January 2027.

Novo AI lets owners ask questions in plain language, locate transactions, examine spending patterns, and receive personalized recommendations. Instead of remembering a merchant’s exact name, an owner could describe an expense by its approximate amount, purpose, and timing.

The Novo Banking Agent’s product page explains that answers draw on Novo’s help material and the customer’s account, with links to sources or relevant account screens. That connection matters: a general-purpose chatbot can explain cash flow, but useful account assistance needs access to the actual payments and balances behind the question.

Owners can choose between access to help content, help and navigation, or all account data. Novo indicates the in-app agent can prepare tasks and suggest settings, but cannot independently move money or make changes without approval. It can also direct users to human support.

“The businesses growing with AI run leaner and move faster, and they’re going to expect the same from their bank,” noted Jackson Barnes, Novo’s CEO, in the announcement. Novo is a financial technology manufacturer rather than a bank; its banking services are provided by Middlesex Federal Savings, F.A.

According to recent reports, the announcement also includes the Novo Agent API. Its developer-facing website describes a closed beta for Novo account owners, rather than unrestricted general availability.

It has been revealed that the beta supports reading account information, transactions, bookkeeping data, and card details, as well as freezing a card. Access uses individually scoped keys and short-lived tokens. Developers work through REST requests and JSON, common formats that allow software to request information and receive structured responses.

In a recent development, novo also marks externally written text as untrusted. This is relevant when an AI tool reads merchant descriptions or other free-text records: information retrieved from a financial system should not automatically become an instruction to the agent.

In a recent development, money movement and payee operations are labeled as planned capabilities, with owner approval on a phone required. The beta does not include an official Model Context Protocol server, webhooks, or a sandbox. These distinctions separate what developers can build now from the broader agentic banking roadmap.

Novo Payroll, powered by Gusto, brings W-2 employee and 1099 contractor payments into the account interface. It includes payroll tax withholding and filing, paystubs, and year-end forms. Existing business information can prefill setup, reducing repeated entry across systems.

For an owner, the practical benefit is seeing a payroll obligation alongside the money available to cover it. Connecting those records can make an approaching cash shortfall easier to spot before a payment is due.

In a recent development, novo Tax uses april’s embedded tax-filing technology. Eligible sole proprietors and LLCs can prepare and file federal and state returns without filing fees, with Novo covering those costs. Categorized income and expenses help prefill the return, while an AI guide works through follow-up questions. Consumers review the information before filing; transactions left uncategorized are not included in that transfer. Filing for the 2026 tax year opens in January 2027.

The wider launch includes instant Novo-to-Novo payments, connected external accounts, more than ten native integrations, expanded credit card features, installment loans, and revenue-based funding. These are different financial products, with eligibility determined separately, rather than a single pool of automatically available credit.

In a recent development, novo’s business savings account offers a variable 2% annual percentage yield with a $50,000 opening minimum and a $50,000 end-of-day balance required to earn interest. The announcement’s savings rate therefore applies to businesses able to maintain that balance, rather than every checking customer.

Novo’s analysis also compared cash positions between customers paying for AI tools and those who were not. Among businesses with at least $250,000 in annual revenue, AI-paying customers ended the Q3 2025-to-Q3 2026 comparison period with twice as much cash on hand. For businesses above $500,000 in revenue, the difference was fourfold.

According to recent reports, those comparisons show an association, not proof that AI spending produced the additional cash. Businesses adopting the tools may differ in size, sector, growth, or financial management. The announcement does not provide an experimental design that isolates AI’s contribution.

Industry observers note that the product launch addresses a more concrete question: whether connecting financial records can make everyday business administration less fragmented. Novo’s approach combines account-grounded answers, embedded service providers, and controlled access for outside software. Its usefulness will depend on whether owners can turn those connections into faster, accurate decisions while retaining control over their money.

Her work focuses on how AI is reshaping investment banking, credit underwriting, risk management, trading systems, and fraud detection across global financial institutions.

It has been revealed that with a precise and quantitative perspective, Vera examines how machine learning models are applied to market analysis, credit scoring, anti-money laundering, and operational efficiency in banking. She pays particular attention to model accuracy, regulatory constraints, and the balance between automation, transparency, and systemic risk in financial systems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that airspeed is opening early access to Airbot, a proactive sales assistant that brings deal updates, meeting preparation and follow-up priorities into WhatsApp and iMessage. The product is designed for founders, investors and revenue teams who want a single conversation with an assistant that understands their work across connected tools.

Owners can join the Airbot waitlist as Airspeed begins the rollout. The company indicates the assistant learns how a user and their organization sell, then surfaces actions that need attention before someone submits a request.

The premise addresses a familiar problem in sales software: information is spread across calendars, email, messaging and customer relationship management systems, while the work of deciding what matters still falls to the person moving between them.

It has been revealed that airbot connects to tools selected by the user, including Google Workspace, Slack and Salesforce. Instead of sending people to another dashboard, it delivers tailored text updates that they can answer with a question or a task.

It has been revealed that airspeed’s launch example combines a daily call schedule with a change in a customer relationship. The assistant flags that a key supporter at an account has left, identifies a replacement and offers to prepare an introduction before an upcoming meeting. The point is to connect an event to a useful next step, rather than produce another isolated notification.

“Salespeople, founders and VCs live on their phones and Airbot meets them in their messages, surfacing what matters most into a single conversation with no newly introduced app, dashboard or rollout,” mentioned Adam Liska, CEO and co-founder of Airspeed.

Sources indicate that liska describes the product as learning a organization’s playbook and pipeline over time. That makes the messaging interface one part of the proposition; the other is whether the assistant can maintain enough business context to make its interventions relevant.

The confirmed use cases extend from routine preparation to changes that could affect a deal. Airspeed says Airbot can look up what a customer pays directly from a contract, spot unresolved conversations, refresh a briefing shortly before a call and highlight deals that need attention ahead of a forecast meeting.

Other examples include identifying a lost opportunity worth reopening, reviewing forecast categories across connected sales tools and detecting when an account’s internal champion leaves. These are tasks where timing and context can matter as much as the information itself.

According to recent reports, the assistant’s reach depends on what the user connects. A calendar can provide meeting timing, while a contract or CRM record supplies different context. Bringing those sources together can make an alert more useful, but it also makes accurate retrieval and sensible prioritization central to the experience.

“Most agents right now add to the noise rather than cut through it,” mentioned Devang Agrawal, CTO and co-founder of Airspeed. He said teams need a streamlined assistant that understands context and escalates concerns and opportunities ahead of time.

Airspeed already positions its broader platform around revenue execution. Its product website describes analyzing calls and email, capturing sales qualification information and synchronizing CRM fields with Salesforce or HubSpot.

Recent findings suggest that the firm’s pipeline-execution offering also covers call preparation, drafted follow-ups, next steps and deal-risk alerts. Airbot brings a upcoming messaging interface and proactive-assistant proposition to that wider focus on turning sales information into action.

Sources indicate that that distinction matters for the launch: the capabilities of the established Airspeed platform provide context for the company’s approach, while Airbot itself is entering early access. The product’s public site right now directs prospective customers to a waitlist.

It has been revealed that airspeed claims Airbot does not send an email unless the user asks it to. Owners select which tools it can access and can disconnect them at any time.

These controls separate surfacing a priority from communicating externally on someone’s behalf. An assistant may identify a missing follow-up or prepare a response, while the decision to send it remains consequential for the customer relationship.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer states that it is SOC 2 Type II compliant. Its security documentation describes independently audited controls, encryption in transit and at rest, and enterprise authentication and access-control options for the broader Airspeed platform.

Airspeed was founded in 2022 by Liska and Agrawal, who met while working on applied language-model research at Google DeepMind. The organization’s history records its origins as Glyphic and its rebrand to Airspeed in May 2026, as the product expanded beyond summarizing calls into executing work around them.

The business notes it serves more than 180 customers across 20 countries and has raised more than $25 million, including a $20 million Series A led by DN Capital in June 2026. Those figures describe Airspeed’s wider business, rather than adoption of the fresh Airbot product.

It has been revealed that airbot’s early-access launch tests a straightforward idea: a sales assistant becomes more useful when it brings the next relevant action into a conversation people already use. Its success will depend on the quality of those priorities and the follow-through they enable. Interested users can join the Airbot waitlist.

Breaking: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • According to recent reports, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

According to recent reports, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post indicates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

In a recent development, meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that prepares, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the latest modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Industry observers note that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

In a recent development, the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Industry observers note that the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

It has been revealed that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

It has been revealed that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

It has been revealed that the language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Industry observers note that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section indicates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Industry observers note that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Industry observers note that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

According to recent reports, the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

In a recent development, we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

It has been revealed that we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

According to recent reports, you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

It has been revealed that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Microsoft Releases .NET 11: C# 15 Union Types, Native AOT CLI Host, and CoreCLR by Default in MAUI.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

Last week, Microsoft has released .NET 11, the latest version of its development platform, together with C# 15, F# 11, ASP.NET Core 11, .NET MAUI, and Entity Framework Core 11. The release is a Standard Term Support (STS) version and will be supported for two years.

As stated in the announcement, .NET 10 remains the Long-Term Support option, while .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on the same day, November 10, 2026. The release coincided with this year's .NET Conf, held from November 10 to 13.

According to recent reports, C# 15 is the default language version for projects that target .NET 11. It adds union types, declared with the union keyword, and the compiler checks switch expressions over them for exhaustiveness. Closed hierarchies limit derivation to the declaring assembly.

The language also gains collection expression arguments, extension indexers, and labeled break and continue statements, while the memory safety work stays in preview. F# 11, according to the release, lowers compiler memory use and reduces collection allocations in FSharp.Core.

According to recent reports, in the SDK, the CLI now starts through a Native AOT host by default and keeps the MSBuild server warm between invocations. The dotnet test command gains run-level timeouts and failure limits, and container publishing can produce reproducible digests. In the runtime, Runtime Async remains a preview and is turned on with a feature flag.

The JIT removes more bounds checks and improves devirtualization. As described in the documentation, the release also raises the minimum hardware requirements, and the x86/x64 baseline moves to x86-64-v2.

Industry observers note that the libraries add Zstandard compression to System.IO.Compression, new Process APIs for running a process and capturing its output, and four in-memory stream adapters. System.Text.Json supports C# unions and JSON Lines output, and LINQ gains a FullJoin operator.

Recent findings suggest that ASP.NET Core 11 adds asynchronous validation and generates OpenAPI 3.2 documents by default, which the release notes list as a breaking change. SignalR can refresh authentication without reconnecting.

Blazor receives a CacheView component for static server-side rendering, client-side validation for static SSR forms, and an opt-in automatic circuit pause for inactive tabs. An experimental package with AI components for Blazor is also available.

In a recent development, .NET MAUI now uses CoreCLR as the default runtime, with Mono still available and Native AOT as an opt-in option. As reported, XAML Incremental Hot Reload is on by default for Debug builds, XAML namespace declarations are implicit, and the Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships.

It has been revealed that entity Framework Core 11 requires .NET 11. It generates fewer unnecessary joins, translates FullJoin, supports complex types and JSON columns with TPT and TPC inheritance, and adds experimental vector search for SQL Server.

Other changes in this release are the dotnet fresh mcpserver template, the dotnetup toolchain manager in public preview, .NET Skills for coding agents, opt-in modern visual styles in Windows Forms, and reliability fixes in WPF.

On Reddit, the reaction was mixed. Several developers welcomed union types as a replacement for hand-written result classes, and others said that .NET 11 and .NET 10 share the same end-of-support date.

In a recent development, the most upvoted comments argued that AI coding tools have made upcoming releases feel less exciting. Other owners criticized the code fix for non-exhaustive switch expressions and asked for the decimal conversion change to be more visible.

For interested readers, the full release notes and the list of breaking changes are available in the official .NET 11 documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Genesis AI announced a $500 million Series A on November 17, 2026, to accelerate development and deployment of its general-purpose robots, beginning in manufacturing and logistics, and to expand its team.

The financing follows its July 1, 2025 emergence from stealth with $105 million in seed funding co-led by Eclipse and Khosla Ventures. Genesis is now directing capital toward both its underlying robotics technology and the industrial deployments intended to make that technology commercially useful.

Genesis’s strategy spans GENE, its robotics foundation model; Eno, its robot hardware; and the deployment operation connecting the machines to customer workflows. The tech giant says owning all three allows real-world failures to inform model training and subsequent hardware, while coordinating hardware and model development and using manufacturing scale to improve reliability and reduce costs.

Recent findings suggest that that design is intended to address reliability across complete jobs rather than isolated demonstrations. Genesis’s reliability example multiplies the risk across a workflow: when each of 20 steps has a 99% success rate, the probability of an error-free run falls to 82%. The example explains why the organization treats intelligence, hardware and deployment as a shared reliability problem, with one weak component potentially limiting the entire system.

Industry observers note that the model’s training pipeline begins with a human-scale robotic hand and a data-collection glove fitted with tactile-sensing electronic skin. In its May 2026 GENE-26.5 announcement, Genesis described a 1:1:1 mapping among the human hand, glove and robot hand, designed to turn human skills into training data. People wearing the glove during ordinary work can generate job-based data, supplemented by egocentric video from camera-wearing people and human-focused internet video.

Genesis reported that the glove’s hardware cost was 100 times lower than typical options and that internal testing highlighted up to five times greater data-collection efficiency, with better data quality than traditional teleoperation.

The company’s GENE-26.5 demonstrations spanned cooking, pipetting and liquid transfer, wire bundling and grasping several objects simultaneously. GENE serves as a shared robotics foundation model, while Genesis World extends the training loop into simulation. The simulator exposes failures across millions of scenarios, using them to guide additional data collection and model changes. Once Eno is deployed, real-world failures can also become simulation cases, training data and hardware revisions.

Genesis unveiled Eno on June 16, 2026, as its first general-purpose robot. A wheeled base supports jointed panels that adjust height and reach and fold for storage, while its two arms use the manufacturer’s human-scale dexterous hands. The design prioritizes mobility and manipulation over a fully human appearance.

Industry observers note that genesis describes Eno and GENE as an integrated system capable of managing multi-step workflows, including keeping production lines stocked and preparing facilities for the next shift. An optional screen is planned to show nearby workers the robot’s intent, reasoning and operational state.

According to recent reports, at that unveiling, Genesis noted it planned to begin production and targeted customer deployments by the end of 2026. Manufacturing, logistics and laboratory customers were first in line, followed by hotels and hospitals, with home and outdoor applications later. The Series A roadmap maintains that sequence, with expansion beyond factories and warehouses dependent on improvements in capability and affordability.

A separate June 16 partnership announcement with LG CNS provides a potential deployment route. The proposal calls for evaluating and validating robots for manufacturing and logistics at LG operations in the United States and within LG CNS’s industrial customer base, initially in the U.S. A subsequent pilot is intended to create a deployment playbook covering workflow documentation, data collection, further model training and validation before a broader rollout.

According to recent reports, the new funding makes those industrial deployments the critical test of Genesis’s approach. Its broader expansion depends on converting dexterity demonstrations into reliable daily workflows, then using the resulting failures and operational data to improve subsequent models and robots.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • Sources indicate that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Sources indicate that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All fresh data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

According to recent reports, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

In a recent development, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Recent findings suggest that proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been revealed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

It has been revealed that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team revealed the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In a recent development, in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Sources indicate that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!
