Spotify Makes Artist Profile Protection Available to All Artists

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spotify made Artist Profile Protection available to all artists on November 17, 2026, expanding an optional control that lets them review releases delivered under their names and remove incorrect associations before those releases affect their profiles, statistics or listener recommendations.
  • The expansion tackles a distribution problem that predates generative AI: metadata mix-ups, shared artist names and malicious uploads can place music on the wrong profile across streaming services.
  • Sources indicate that the feature is designed to control attribution on Spotify, not to determine whether audio was generated by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify made Artist Profile Protection available to all artists on November 17, 2026, expanding an optional control that lets them review releases delivered under their names and remove incorrect associations before those releases affect their profiles, statistics or listener recommendations.

The expansion tackles a distribution problem that predates generative AI: metadata mix-ups, shared artist names and malicious uploads can place music on the wrong profile across streaming services. Spotify indicates easy-to-produce AI tracks have aggravated the problem, which can distort an artist’s catalog and statistics, interfere with Release Radar and change how fans discover the music.

Sources indicate that the feature is designed to control attribution on Spotify, not to determine whether audio was generated by AI. After an artist opts in, Spotify sends an email when a delivery carries that artist’s name. The artist can review eligible releases and remove an incorrect association; doing nothing lets the release go live as scheduled with the artist listed.

Industry observers note that A rejected release will not list that artist, appear on their profile, feed their statistics or enter recommendations to their listeners. The decision applies only to Spotify, so the same release can remain misattributed elsewhere and the artist may still need to contact a label or distributor.

Artist team administrators and editors can manage the feature through desktop artist settings or the mobile app’s music tab. The Help Center documentation describes two modes: Review releases lets music go live unless the artist removes their association, while Block releases, available only to some artists, requires approval before the artist can be listed.

It has been revealed that spotify recommends Block for artists with common names or repeated mismatches who can actively manage their catalogs. Legitimate releases can be delayed or blocked if nobody approves them. Artists can act before release or for up to 28 days afterward, while approvals can take up to 24 hours to process.

It has been revealed that review coverage includes main and featured artists, remixers and actors, plus composers, orchestras and conductors on classical releases. In Block mode, an artist key lets trusted distributors pre-approve legitimate deliveries. The key should not be posted publicly; it may not work with every provider, and releases from some providers may be ineligible for removal or approval.

Recent findings suggest that spotify says it tested Artist Profile Protection for several months with thousands of artists, including Samia, Diplo, Searows and Dave East. Robbie Mackey of Grand Jury Music, speaking for Samia’s team, remarked, “We’re glad Spotify is giving us more control over what appears under her name.”.

The wider rollout fulfills a plan set out in an October 20, 2026 platform patch, which still called the tool a beta and promised access for all artists by year-end.

Recent findings suggest that in that update, Spotify reported taking more than 50 million slop and spam tracks out of recommendations during 2026. Separately, more than 75 million spammy tracks had been removed from the platform altogether for serious or repeated rule violations.

That enforcement is distinct from profile review. Spotify indicates its recommendation systems combine listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata and multiple third-party AI-detection tools because no single signal catches every instance of slop or spam. The organization also acknowledges that AI detection has limitations.

It has been revealed that artist Profile Protection is separate from Spotify’s voice-impersonation policy, which covers unauthorized replicas of an artist’s voice, including AI clones. Spotify requires a claim from the artist or a representative because it cannot determine whether a particular use is a cleared sample or collaboration. After reviewing a submission, Spotify can remove music that violates the policy.

The voice policy can apply even when the impersonated artist is absent from the credits or the uploader presents the track as an AI rendition, with exceptions including certain parodies.

Sources indicate that for artists, the upcoming control moves a consequential decision—whether a release should shape their public catalog and recommendations—into their own review queue. Its reach is narrower than a deepfake takedown system: it depends on artist action and provider eligibility, and it cannot correct attribution on rival services or settle whether a voice was used without permission.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post reveals you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

According to recent reports, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Sources indicate that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

In a recent development, every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

It has been revealed that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Sources indicate that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Proposal for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

In a recent development, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Industry observers note that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Recent findings suggest that beam's config defines an expert-parallel initiative. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Sources indicate that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Recent findings suggest that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

According to recent reports, beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

Industry observers note that on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Recent findings suggest that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

It has been revealed that * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

It has been revealed that you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Sources indicate that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

It has been revealed that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

It has been revealed that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

In a recent development, sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Revision: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

It has been revealed that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

It has been revealed that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

Sources indicate that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one revision behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

It has been revealed that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Sources indicate that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Industry observers note that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

In a recent development, decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Recent findings suggest that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Industry observers note that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Recent findings suggest that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability.

Nov 17, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Offline evaluations remain an crucial part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

It has been revealed that however, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. Upcoming user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify newly introduced scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors.Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of customers before rolling it out more widely.

According to recent reports, this is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

Sources indicate that datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that however, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model highlighted estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

According to recent reports, datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

Sources indicate that the important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AMD revealed on November 17, 2026 that it had completed its acquisition of Taalas, a Toronto-based developer of model-specific inference chips.
  • That estimate included contingent consideration of up to approximately $1.4 billion.
  • In a recent development, the closing follows the definitive agreement AMD declared on August 6, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AMD revealed on November 17, 2026 that it had completed its acquisition of Taalas, a Toronto-based developer of model-specific inference chips. A November 4, 2026 quarterly filing valued the then-pending cash-and-stock transaction at approximately $2.9 billion.

That estimate included contingent consideration of up to approximately $1.4 billion. AMD had expected the acquisition to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, placing the completed transaction within its disclosed timetable.

In a recent development, the closing follows the definitive agreement AMD declared on August 6, 2026. Founded in 2023, Taalas develops technology that AMD describes as optimizing inference dataflows and reducing compute and memory bottlenecks associated with general-purpose architectures.

According to recent reports, taalas indicates its platform can turn a previously unseen AI model into custom silicon in two months, with storage and computation merged on one chip at DRAM-level density. The design targets the bottleneck created by moving model data between separate memory and compute components. The resulting system does not require high-bandwidth memory (HBM), advanced packaging, 3D stacking, liquid cooling or high-speed I/O.

Industry observers note that its HC1 technology demonstrator hard-wires Llama 3.1 8B and is built on TSMC’s 6-nanometer process. The chip has an 815-square-millimeter die and 53 billion transistors, while the server configuration is listed at 2.5 kilowatts. Taalas reports 17,000 tokens per second per user on the model, measured in its own labs with 1,000-token input and 1,000-token output sequences.

Recent findings suggest that HC1 retains configurable context-window sizing and supports fine-tuning through low-rank adapters despite being largely hard-wired. Taalas states its first-generation quantization combines 3-bit and 6-bit parameters and introduces some quality degradation relative to GPU benchmarks; its second-generation design adopts standard 4-bit floating-point formats to address those limitations while maintaining high speed and efficiency.

AMD plans to integrate Taalas’s technology into its accelerator roadmap and develop system-level solutions alongside Instinct GPUs. The surrounding portfolio includes EPYC CPUs, ROCm software and the Helios rack-scale system. The acquisition also expands AMD’s engineering presence in Canada.

According to recent reports, “AI inference is evolving rapidly, and customers need a broad range of compute solutions optimized for their workloads. With Taalas now part of AMD, we’re expanding our ability to deliver differentiated inference performance and efficiency, while strengthening our full-stack AI platform,” stated Vamsi Boppana, senior vice president of AMD’s Artificial Intelligence Group.

In a recent development, the acquisition puts both sides of Taalas’s design trade-off inside AMD’s accelerator roadmap: reported speed and efficiency gains from model-specific silicon, and a second-generation effort to address the first design’s quantization compromises. AMD’s planned system-level integration is where those specialized designs will meet Instinct GPUs and the rest of its inference stack.

Tech Report: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a newly introduced backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a newly introduced backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

It has been revealed that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron people use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Recent findings suggest that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

It has been revealed that parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

In a recent development, nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Recent findings suggest that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Sources indicate that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Science Corporation unveiled on November 17, 2026 that it raised a $400 million Series D to expand availability of its PRIMA retinal implant in Europe, prepare for a US launch, and increase investment in its biohybrid neural-interface program.
  • Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech participated, among other investors.
  • Recent findings suggest that PRIMA is a retinal implant being studied for geographic atrophy caused by dry age-related macular degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation unveiled on November 17, 2026 that it raised a $400 million Series D to expand availability of its PRIMA retinal implant in Europe, prepare for a US launch, and increase investment in its biohybrid neural-interface program.

Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech participated, among other investors. The round brings total capital raised since Science’s founding in 2021 to more than $900 million. The manufacturer will also expand its research, manufacturing and operational infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that PRIMA is a retinal implant being studied for geographic atrophy caused by dry age-related macular degeneration. Science describes it as the first brain-computer interface CE marked in the European Union to restore form vision—the ability to read letters, numbers and words—for patients blinded by certain types of late-stage macular degeneration. It is registered for supply in the United Kingdom and is not approved or available for sale in any other country.

In a recent development, the implant contains 378 light-powered pixels that convert light from the system’s glasses into signals that stimulate retinal cells. The glasses combine a front-facing camera with an eye-facing projector that shines light precisely onto the implant. The design is intended to replicate the function of light-sensitive cells that have been lost.

Sources indicate that at 12 months, 80% of patients in the PRIMA clinical study revealed clinically meaningful improvement in visual acuity, and 84% reported reading letters, numbers and words at home with the system, according to Science’s product page. The reported efficacy results include the use of digital zoom and contrast.

In a recent development, in a July 22, 2026 announcement, Science remarked PRIMA had received two FDA Humanitarian Use Device designations. The program provides expedited review for devices treating rare diseases or conditions, but designation is not marketing approval: PRIMA must still be reviewed and approved through a Humanitarian Device Exemption. One designation covers blindness in both eyes caused by an advanced subset of geographic atrophy, without vision loss from other eye diseases; the other covers vision loss from Stargardt disease, a rare inherited retinal disease. The US approval process remains underway.

It has been revealed that science’s biohybrid architecture takes a different approach from the retinal implant: it anchors hundreds of thousands of engineered neurons to a device and uses their projections to form connections with neurons in the brain. MicroLEDs stimulate the embedded neurons, which are modified through optogenetics so they can be activated by light, while electrodes record their activity. Science states the architecture can provide orders of magnitude more bandwidth than current devices while avoiding the damage and limitations associated with inserting wires into the brain.

The manufacturer describes language and communication, motor control, and learning and reasoning after brain injuries as potential research applications for the technology.

The financing therefore supports two distinct stages of development: commercial expansion of a retinal implant still seeking US approval, and continued development of a separate neural-interface architecture whose therapeutic uses remain research objectives.

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Recent findings suggest that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

It has been revealed that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel indicates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Industry observers note that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

In a recent development, small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Sources indicate that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them latest paths through Metal:.

Recent findings suggest that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Recent findings suggest that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

According to recent reports, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Industry observers note that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A substantial thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Industry observers note that 1. Why is email marketing crucial?Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.2. What is benefits of email marketing?Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:Better brand recognitionStatistics of what works bestMore salesTargeted audienceMore traffic to your products/services/newsletterBuild credibilityMost  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide. 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.5. How do I write a decent subject line?The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free. 6. Is email marketing still effective?Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also patch them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your owners' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. InfoQ Homepage News Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

Qwik, the resumable JavaScript framework originally created at Builder.io, has released its 2.0 Release Candidate, targeting a rewrite of how the framework encodes resumable state in server-rendered HTML and introducing experimental out-of-order streaming. The RC was published on 1st October 2026 as @qwik.dev/core@2.0.0-rc.0, around two years and eight months after the initial Towards Qwik 2.0 design article.

Industry observers note that in v1, Qwik propagated state updates by sprinkling HTML comment markers such as and throughout the rendered body to flag component boundaries and the text nodes a signal should update. That approach forced a single ordered write pass, added CPU and memory overhead, and made out-of-order streaming impossible because a slow fetch blocked everything after it. In v2 the comments are gone, with state and virtual node information instead compressed into two.

The Financial Rules AI Agents Break When Chasing Results

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, it’s a shame, because I would actually like to; while my HSBC account indicates you the most recent transactions in descending reverse order as a ‘front page’ feed after login, my ING bank account buries this information in a ghastly and arcane process of requesting PDFs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the sole installation of agentic AI that I have on my LAN is Codex, running in a Windows 10 VM on the large machine learning server. It makes me nervous enough that Codex can see and interact with precious data on LAN shares, if it should ever get bored with creating and maintaining the VM-located program that I have concentrated its efforts on over the last month.

I certainly cannot imagine letting this enthusiastic but too-often maladroit construct loose on my bank accounts.

In a recent development, it’s a shame, because I would actually like to; while my HSBC account indicates you the most recent transactions in descending reverse order as a ‘front page’ feed after login, my ING bank account buries this information in a ghastly and arcane process of requesting PDFs. Thus, when I get a cryptic iPhone alert about some new transaction, considerable sleuthing is needed to locate what it was (the initial message is always truncated).

So it would be a boon if I could generate a Python program to automate this, and have that info at my fingertips in an instant, HSBC-style. Or, in the likely event that Python gets a 403 response, to have an AI agent try it instead,.

But seriously, to hell with that – as it stands, for the moment, I’ll endure that and any other amount of friction before AI gets to explore that space of my life at will.

In the case of HSBC, the point is or soon will be moot, as it is one of the British banks – together with Nationwide, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – that last week confirmed that it is seeking to ban agents from connecting to clients’ accounts (a move also echoed last week by United Airlines).

This all seems part of The Great Retrenchment that I observe in the world in this period: sites that enforce logins, and cloister data away from the voracious AI crawlers; and domains that in greater numbers are adopting CAPTCHA-walls, determined to deter automated crawlers and non-humans from seeking access.

At this rate of retreat, I calculate that physical newspapers and magazines may unexpectedly resurrect in a couple of years’ time.

I guess I’m part of the problem: I have recently started experimenting with web-scraping,  and I must confess that, viewed as a hobby or casual pastime, it feels like getting into vinyl in 1985, or Filofaxes in 1990 – very much the ‘scrag end’ of what is becoming an increasingly reviled and repelled pursuit.

In my case I am using a scraper-enclosed web browser – in the form of Reading Desk – to recreate the fifty or so Reddit RSS feeds that went dark a few days ago, among other projects.

Depending on the task, I often have to resort to proxies and VPN connections, as well as headless browsers such as Playwright; in the most extreme case I right now run, I have twin Firefox profiles, each with a different country IP address, polling a particularly 403-prone auction site in order to recreate the RSS listings that the site shut down a few years ago; because I’m not taking The Great Retrenchment lying down.

Industry observers note that I can see no reason why people determined to access financial services through agentic AI can’t do the same thing, and I’m sure they will. So long as HSBC sees a full-headed, consumer-looking Chrome of Firefox browser accessing its site at human-looking speed, I’m certain that AI agents will learn to pass any of its captchas, in order to authenticate and do their masters’ bidding.

Therefore the banning of such services, no doubt soon to enter the banks’ T&Cs, won’t actually stop agentic access, but instead will just indemnify banks; and to that extent, it will serves as a mani pulite disassociation from the practice.

It has been revealed that that mentioned, I think the banks are genuinely scared of engaging with ‘alien’ agentic AI, and that they’re right to be scared. The ascent of agentic AI is raising concerns about security in one of the most critical domains besides nuclear power, and the reputation of financial agents needs to rise considerably if they are ever to be allowed proactivity across financial services.

All this came to mind today while reading a new study from China, which found that AI agents managing simulated investment portfolios begin to break trading rules when given increasingly demanding performance targets.

According to recent reports, A simple schema for the paper’s objective – to determine whether relatively itinerant AI instances would obey rules under different types of pressure. Source.

All eight models, including OpenAI’s GPT-5.4, Google’s Gemini-2.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-V3.2, initially obeyed the rules; but once the targets could no longer be met legally, the agents broke the rules nearly 90% of the time, on average.

In a recent development, GPT-5.4 was among the worst offenders, breaking the trading rules in every decision after the targets were raised. This continued through the remaining 20 rounds of the experiment, even though the model had followed the rules throughout the first ten.

According to recent reports, when directly asked to break an investment rule, all eight AI models refused. But when told to make more money, two of them broke that same rule in over 90% of cases, even though nobody had instructed them to do anything illegal.

‘All evaluated models exhibit safety violations, with substantial variation across models, constraints, and economic settings. The source of pressure also matters.

‘The same constraint can lead to different behavior depending on whether pressure comes from the user, another actor, or the agent’s own task objective, and violations can arise without an explicit unsafe request.

‘Finally, initial compliance may not persist under sustained pressure.

‘As performance targets increase, some agents begin to violate previously respected constraints, while others remain compliant. These findings reveal that stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation are needed before LLM agents can be reliably deployed in economic environments.’.

The newly introduced study offers a benchmark called EconSafeBench, created through a combination of AI-generated test cases, automated evaluation and human review, and with code and data made public.

A series of economic scenarios was first defined by the researchers, with each test specifying the agent’s role, its objective, the applicable restrictions, and the actions that would constitute a violation.

According to recent reports, claude Sonnet 4.6 was then used to generate test cases. Each case included a description of the situation, instructions for the agent, and precise criteria for determining whether a rule had been broken. Three versions of each scenario were produced, with the source of pressure varied, even as the underlying decision and restrictions remained unchanged.

Sources indicate that after this, the generated cases were evaluated by Gemini 3 Pro using a 16-point scoring system. The four aspects assessed were the accuracy of the proposed violation; its grounding in real institutional rules; whether the outcome could be objectively determined; and whether permitted and prohibited actions were clearly distinguished.

Cases that failed to meet the required standard were returned for revision, and the remaining cases reviewed by the researchers. A random 20% sample was independently checked by a second reviewer. Thus, the final benchmark contained 828 tests, averaging 14.35 out of a possible 16 points.

It has been revealed that the scenarios were spread across 53 combinations of financial situations, safety restrictions and sources of pressure. Of the three types of pressure represented, 38% involved deception, 35% involved breaking established rules, 15% involved discrimination, and 12% involved privacy violations:.

It has been revealed that distribution of the 828 benchmark tests. The inner ring indicates the three sources of pressure, the middle ring shows the types of rule-breaking tested, and the outer ring shows the five financial settings. Percentages indicate each category’s share of the tests.

The tests were also distributed across five economic settings, with the largest share devoted to access control (28%), followed by lending (23%), market manipulation (22%), portfolio execution (15%), and portfolio management (12%).

The types of misconduct tested varied according to the setting. Access-control scenarios covered all four categories of violation, while portfolio management focused mainly on exceeding investment limits, and providing misleading reports.

All eight models were tested using the same LangGraph-based ReAct framework, with tools that allowed them to perform actions in simulated economic environments. Each action was recorded, along with its effect on the environment, in order to easily identify any rule violations, and most were detected automatically by checking the actions against numerical limits.

Three types of misleading language, involving omitted information, downplaying misconduct and profiling owners, were assessed by Claude Opus 4.6, external to the eight model families under test (see Tests below). The main metric was the violation rate (VR), measuring the percentage of actions that broke the rules. Cases where agents took no action were excluded, and measured separately.

For tests involving increasing pressure, Dynamic Pressure Amplification (DPA, which indicates how much more or less likely agents were to obey the rules as performance demands increased) was used to compare compliance against tests with fixed pressure. A score below 1 indicated reduced compliance under pressure, while a score above 1 indicated improved compliance.

Eight models were evaluated: GPT-5.4; GPT-5.4-mini; Gemini-2.5-Flash; o3-mini; DeepSeek-V3.2; Qwen3-Max; GLM-5; and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Each experiment was run with the three random seeds 42, 43 and 44.

According to recent reports, the first round of tests established how frequently the eight models broke the rules across the benchmark’s various financial scenarios. None completed the tests without violations, though considerable differences were observed: GLM-5 performed best, breaking the rules in 8.5% of its executed decisions, followed closely by GPT-5.4 at 10.7%:.

Test results showing how frequently eight AI models violated financial rules. Lower percentages indicate safer behavior, with 0% representing no violations. GLM-5 recorded the fewest violations (8.5%), while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct recorded the most (40.6%).

Recent findings suggest that the other models performed considerably worse, breaking financial rules in roughly a quarter of their decisions. These violations included exceeding investment limits, making unauthorized transactions, manipulating markets, misleading clients or regulators, discriminating against customers, and improperly disclosing private information.

Google’s Gemini-2.5-Flash violated the rules in 24.2% of its decisions, DeepSeek-V3.2 in 25.2%, and OpenAI’s o3-mini in 28.8%.

The worst result was recorded by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, which violated the rules in 40.6% of its decisions –  almost five times the rate observed for GLM-5.

In another test, the effect of different sources of pressure was examined. Each scenario was presented in three forms: a violation could be independently chosen while an objective was being pursued; it could be explicitly requested by the user; or pressure to commit it could be applied by another actor in the simulated environment.

Even when no violation had been requested, rules were broken at rates ranging from 10.1% for GLM-5 to 29.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. In some cases, safer behavior was actually observed when a rule was explicitly requested to be broken:.

Test results comparing rule-breaking under three sources of pressure. Type I represents violations chosen by the agent while pursuing its objective, Type II violations explicitly requested by the user, and Type III violations encouraged by another actor. Lower percentages indicate safer behavior, with the lowest rate in each column shown in bold.

In regard to the portfolio-management tests, when the models were directly asked to exceed an investment position limit, the request was refused by all eight. Yet when a return target was assigned, and the means of achieving it were left to the models, the same limit was exceeded in 92% and 94% of cases by two models, while rates above 30% were recorded for two others.

Thus, a prohibited action could be refused when requested directly, while the same action could still be chosen independently when it provided a route toward an assigned objective.

Finally†, the effect of ‘mounting pressure’ was tested, by making the agents’ targets progressively harder to meet.

In the portfolio-management test, all eight models initially stayed within the rules; however, when the target was raised beyond what could be achieved legally, the average violation rate suddenly jumped to 87.5%, and remained at 84% in the final phase. For seven models, this happened almost immediately, with violation rates going from zero to 90-100% in a single phase:.

Recent findings suggest that how escalating pressure affected rule-breaking, with violation rates compared between control runs with achievable targets, and experimental runs where targets were progressively increased. A DPA below 1 indicates that violations increased under pressure; 1 indicates no violations in either group.

Sources indicate that A similar result was obtained when the models were asked to control labor costs. Once the target could no longer be met while paying the legal minimum wage, five of the eight models began setting illegal wages. By the final phase, violation rates for these models ranged from 46.7% to 100%. Meanwhile, the control tests, where the targets were kept within legal reach, produced no violations.

This suggests, the authors contend, that compliance can collapse very quickly when agents are given goals that can’t be reached without breaking the rules.

Sources indicate that everyone wants a factotum, but not everyone wants to arbitrarily hand out power of attorney – and particularly not to the current state of the art in LLMs. The more you use them, the more you study them, the more they demonstrate their shortcomings, the more insane it seems to even consider giving them access to privileged financial domains.

Sources indicate that nonetheless these insights and standpoints are not shared by all, and hold-outs such as myself are in an uneven three-way conflict between the AI companies that need to capitalize very quickly or risk to perish, and the millions of firms racing enthusiastically for pole position in the AI job displacement-tables because of shareholder imperatives and obligations. I know where the money is in that contention.

* Titled ‘When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds’.

† There are two other tests in the paper which we have not been able to cover due to lack of space and time, so please check out the source PDF if you’re interested in these (in my opinion) less significant results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Sources indicate that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Sources indicate that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Industry observers note that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the latest provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

According to recent reports, and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Sources indicate that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

It has been revealed that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.
